title: Belief Counseling - Lie Finder master list
note: Built by tools/build_lie_finder_list.py from the belief cards. Do not edit by hand; re-run the script.

beliefs.belief: My body has betrayed me.
beliefs.origins: A diagnosis, a flare, or a body that no longer cooperates can feel like treachery from the one thing we thought we could count on. Anger and grief at the body are natural, and over time they can turn into resentment, fear, or a sense of being at war with ourselves.
client_words: My body is the enemy.
It let me down.
I cannot trust it anymore.
I am at war with myself.
It is ruining my life.
I hate what it has become.

beliefs.belief: I am nothing but my illness.
beliefs.origins: Appointments, symptoms, medication schedules, and other people’s questions can make illness the center of life. The label can replace the name.
client_words: I am just a patient.
My illness defines me.
Nothing else about me matters.
People only see my condition.
I am my diagnosis.
I have no identity apart from this.

beliefs.belief: I will never feel well again.
beliefs.origins: Long illness wears down hope. After many treatments, setbacks, and bad days, the mind starts to treat the present as permanent.
client_words: This will never end.
I will always feel this way.
There is no hope for recovery.
Good days are a trick.
What is the point of trying?
I have already tried everything.

beliefs.belief: I am a burden to everyone.
beliefs.origins: Needing help with meals, driving, chores, or finances can make us feel like a weight on those we love. Guilt grows, and some people withdraw so as not to “bother” anyone.
client_words: They would be better off without me.
I am costing them too much.
I should not ask for help.
I am a weight on my family.
They are tired of me.
I wish I did not need anyone.

beliefs.belief: My life is over.
beliefs.origins: A serious diagnosis or permanent change can feel like the end of the life we knew: work, plans, roles, and dreams. Grief for that life is real.
client_words: Everything good is behind me.
There is nothing left to live for.
I am just waiting for the end.
I have no purpose now.
My dreams are dead.
Nothing I do matters.

beliefs.belief: This pain will never end.
beliefs.origins: Pain that lasts for months or years teaches the mind to expect only more pain. Each flare confirms the fear, and hope for relief becomes dangerous.
client_words: It will always be like this.
Relief is impossible.
I cannot survive more years of this.
Hope just makes it worse.
Nothing helps.
This is my life now.

beliefs.belief: I can't take one more day of this.
beliefs.origins: When pain, exhaustion, and discouragement pile up, one more day can seem unbearable. This is a human response to overload, and it can also be a warning sign that more support is needed.
client_words: I cannot go on.
I am at the end.
I have nothing left.
I do not know how I will get through today.
Everything is too much.
I just want it to stop.

beliefs.belief: I can't be happy as long as I hurt.
beliefs.origins: Pain narrows attention, and joy can seem like something that belongs to healthy people. We may stop doing what we enjoy and give up on laughter, connection, and meaning until the pain is gone.
client_words: Happiness is impossible while I hurt.
I do not deserve to enjoy anything.
Joy would be fake.
Hurting people cannot laugh.
I will be happy when the pain stops.
Nothing feels good.

beliefs.belief: If doctors can't find the cause, it must be all in my head.
beliefs.origins: Pain without a clear test result is common. When scans are normal, some patients are dismissed, and many begin to doubt themselves.
client_words: No test shows anything, so I am imagining it.
I must be crazy.
I am exaggerating.
The doctors are right and I am wrong.
I should stop complaining.
Nobody can help me.

beliefs.belief: People think I'm faking.
beliefs.origins: Invisible pain and unpredictable symptoms leave room for doubt. Remarks like “But you look fine,” or being accused of attention-seeking, hurt deeply.
client_words: No one believes me.
They think I am lazy.
I have to prove I am sick.
I cannot explain what it is like.
Everyone doubts me.
I am being judged.

beliefs.belief: Needing medication means I'm weak.
beliefs.origins: Some grew up hearing that real strength means toughing things out. Taking medicine for pain, blood pressure, diabetes, depression, or anxiety can then feel like failure of will.
client_words: Strong people do not need pills.
I should be able to handle this myself.
Medication is a crutch.
I am giving in.
I have failed.
Others manage without it.

beliefs.belief: If this treatment didn't work, nothing will.
beliefs.origins: After a treatment fails, hope takes a hit. Repeated disappointment trains us to expect failure and to stop trying.
client_words: It did not work, so nothing will.
I am a hopeless case.
Why try again?
I am wasting time and money.
There is nothing left.
I am tired of being disappointed.

beliefs.belief: I'll have to take this forever, so I'll never really be well.
beliefs.origins: Long-term medication for chronic conditions can feel like a life sentence. We equate “well” with “needing nothing,” and so we feel permanently broken even when we are doing well.
client_words: I will always be a patient.
I will never be normal.
I am permanently unwell.
Being on medication means I am sick.
I cannot ever stop.
This is a life sentence.

beliefs.belief: Taking medication means I'm not really myself.
beliefs.origins: Some medicines change mood, energy, or thinking. Some people feel flattened or foggy, and others worry that treatment changes their personality or covers their “real” feelings.
client_words: I am not me on this medicine.
It is changing who I am.
My real self is gone.
I feel numb.
I am fake.
I would rather feel pain than lose myself.

beliefs.belief: The side effects prove nothing will ever work for me.
beliefs.origins: Nausea, drowsiness, weight change, or other effects can make us want to quit. After a bad experience with one medication, we may assume all treatments will fail or be intolerable.
client_words: This is intolerable.
Nothing agrees with me.
I will never find something that works.
The cure is worse than the illness.
I am too sensitive.
I should give up.

beliefs.belief: I'm old and useless.
beliefs.origins: Retirement, slower pace, and a culture that prizes youth can make older adults feel invisible. Loss of work, driving, or strength adds to the sense of being no longer needed.
client_words: Nobody needs me.
I have nothing left to give.
Young people do not care what I think.
I am in the way.
I am past my usefulness.
My time is over.

beliefs.belief: My best years are behind me.
beliefs.origins: Nostalgia is natural, but it can harden into believing that the good is over. Losses of health, spouse, or work make the past glow and the future dim.
client_words: The good times are gone.
Nothing will compare.
I peaked long ago.
The future has nothing for me.
Everything was better then.
I just wait for the end.

beliefs.belief: I've lost my purpose.
beliefs.origins: When career, children at home, or health-related roles change, the schedule and the sense of mission change too. Without clear tasks, days feel empty and the question “What am I for?” arises.
client_words: I have no reason to get up.
What am I for now?
No one needs me.
My work is done.
I am just waiting.
I have nothing to live for.

beliefs.belief: I'm too old to change.
beliefs.origins: Habits and beliefs become comfortable over decades, and many hear “you can’t teach an old dog new tricks.” The result is resignation about patterns, health, relationships, or faith.
client_words: I have always been this way.
It is too late for me.
Change is for young people.
I cannot learn new things.
People my age do not change.
Why bother?

beliefs.belief: People are just waiting for me to die.
beliefs.origins: When family talks about wills, care homes, or logistics, an older adult can hear impatience. Isolation, and the absence of visitors, can seem to confirm it.
client_words: They want me gone.
I am in the way.
No one visits.
My family is counting the days.
I am just a problem.
I do not matter anymore.

beliefs.belief: Something is fundamentally wrong with me.
beliefs.origins: Struggling with anxiety, depression, trauma, or other conditions can lead us to see ourselves as defective. Shame and comparison to “normal” people harden into a core belief that something deep inside is broken.
client_words: I am defective.
Normal people do not feel this way.
I was made wrong.
Something is deeply broken in me.
I do not belong with healthy people.
I am the problem.

beliefs.belief: I'm broken and can't be fixed.
beliefs.origins: Years of struggle and failed attempts to feel better can convince us that we are beyond repair. We may stop seeking help or keep it at arm’s length.
client_words: I am beyond repair.
Nothing can fix me.
I have tried everything.
I am a lost cause.
I will always be broken.
Why keep trying?

beliefs.belief: I'll never be normal.
beliefs.origins: Comparison with peers and social ideas of normal produce shame, especially for those with ongoing conditions. Longing to be “normal” can turn into grief or anger.
client_words: Everyone else is normal.
I will always be different.
I do not fit.
Normal people have it easy.
I will never be like them.
I cannot live a regular life.

beliefs.belief: My feelings are facts.
beliefs.origins: Strong emotions feel like truth. When anxious or depressed, thoughts like “I am in danger” or “I am worthless” feel certain.
client_words: If I feel it, it must be true.
I feel worthless, so I am.
I feel doomed, so I am.
My feelings never lie.
Questioning them is denying them.
My gut is always right.

beliefs.belief: I'm going crazy.
beliefs.origins: Racing thoughts, panic, intrusive images, flashbacks, or strange sensations can be frightening and make us fear losing our minds. Fear of “going crazy” often intensifies the very symptoms, and secrecy deepens it.
client_words: I am losing my mind.
I am going to snap.
I cannot control my thoughts.
Something terrible is happening in my head.
I am out of control.
If anyone knew they would lock me up.

beliefs.belief: It runs in my family, so I'm doomed.
beliefs.origins: Watching a parent or relative suffer from a disease, addiction, or mental illness can make us feel that the same fate is sealed. Family patterns are real risk factors, but risk is not destiny, and fear of fate can paralyze us.
client_words: It is in my blood.
I will get it too.
There is no escape.
My family curse will find me.
Why try to prevent it?
I am doomed.

beliefs.belief: I'll end up just like my parent.
beliefs.origins: Seeing a parent struggle with addiction, anger, depression, or illness, we may be terrified of repeating their path. Others tell us, “You’re just like your father,” and we may start acting as if the script is already written.
client_words: I am just like them.
I cannot escape their pattern.
I will make the same mistakes.
It is in my nature.
People expect me to turn out like them.
I am destined to repeat it.

beliefs.belief: I was born defective.
beliefs.origins: A birth condition, learning difference, or inherited trait can feel like proof that we came into the world flawed. Comparisons, medical language, and remarks from others can deepen the feeling of being a mistake.
client_words: I was made wrong.
I am a mistake.
Something went wrong with me from the start.
I was never meant to be.
God made a bad batch.
I have always been broken.

beliefs.belief: It's in my genes, so there's no point trying.
beliefs.origins: When a condition has a genetic component, some conclude that effort, treatment, and habits are pointless. This fatalism can keep people from the very steps that help.
client_words: Nothing I do will make a difference.
Genes decide everything.
Effort is wasted.
I may as well give up.
Why bother with treatment?
I cannot change my biology.

beliefs.belief: I'll pass this on and ruin my children's lives.
beliefs.origins: Parents with inherited conditions often carry deep guilt about the possibility of passing them on. Some avoid having children, and some blame themselves for a child’s struggles.
client_words: It is my fault if they struggle.
I should not have had children.
I have doomed them.
They will suffer because of me.
I cannot forgive myself.
I am a bad parent.

beliefs.belief: I'm not the person I used to be, so I'm less of a person.
beliefs.origins: After a stroke, concussion, or other brain injury, abilities, personality, and speed can change. Family may say, “You’re not the same,” and the loss of who we were can feel like a loss of value.
client_words: I am a shadow of myself.
I am not me anymore.
I have lost who I was.
I am worth less now.
Others miss the old me.
I am a disappointment.

beliefs.belief: I'm stupid now.
beliefs.origins: Slower thinking, trouble finding words, and forgetfulness after injury or illness can feel humiliating, especially to those once quick and capable. Others’ impatience can deepen shame.
client_words: I cannot think anymore.
I used to be smart.
Everyone sees how slow I am.
I am an embarrassment.
I make mistakes all the time.
I am dumb.

beliefs.belief: I'm losing my mind, and nothing can be done.
beliefs.origins: Noticing memory or thinking decline is frightening, especially when family history or a diagnosis is involved. Fear and hopelessness can lead to avoiding doctors, therapy, and support.
client_words: My mind is disappearing.
There is no hope.
It is only going to get worse.
Why get tested?
I cannot stop it.
I will be a burden.

beliefs.belief: If I forget things, people will think less of me.
beliefs.origins: Embarrassment about missing names, repeating stories, or losing track of the conversation can lead to avoiding gatherings or hiding the problem.
client_words: They will think I am senile.
I am embarrassing.
I have to hide it.
I will lose respect.
I should stay home.
They are judging me.

beliefs.belief: I can't learn or grow anymore.
beliefs.origins: After injury or with age, we may stop trying new things because of earlier failures. The brain, however, retains the ability to adapt, and spiritual growth does not depend on speed or memory.
client_words: My learning days are over.
I am stuck where I am.
New things are too hard.
I will never improve.
Therapy is pointless.
I can only go backward.

beliefs.belief: I'm dumb.
beliefs.origins: Struggles with reading, math, attention, or processing can bring years of corrections, low grades, and comparisons. Labels like “slow” or “lazy” stick, and many carry the word “dumb” into adulthood.
client_words: I was born stupid.
Everybody is smarter than me.
I cannot do school.
I will always fail.
Teachers gave up on me.
I am an idiot.

beliefs.belief: I'll always be behind everyone else.
beliefs.origins: Being the last to finish, needing extra help, or taking longer can make us feel in a permanent race we cannot win. Comparison drains energy and joy.
client_words: Everyone passes me.
I will never catch up.
I am always last.
They finish before I start.
I am slow at everything.
There is no use.

beliefs.belief: Why try? I can never succeed.
beliefs.origins: Repeated failure at school, work, or tasks teaches that effort leads nowhere. Learned helplessness protects us from disappointment but also from growth.
client_words: Nothing I do works.
Trying only leads to failure.
I give up.
Others succeed, not me.
I was not made for this.
It is safer not to try.

beliefs.belief: I'm a disappointment to my parents.
beliefs.origins: When grades or milestones are lower than a parent hoped, children can sense disappointment, spoken or not. As adults, they may still hear it, and some parents did say hurtful things.
client_words: I let them down.
They wanted a different child.
I never met their expectations.
They are ashamed of me.
I will never make them proud.
I am a failure to them.

beliefs.belief: Everyone else is better than me.
beliefs.origins: Constant comparison in school, work, and social settings convinces some that they are at the bottom. This belief shrinks risk-taking, friendships, and joy.
client_words: Everyone is better.
I do not measure up.
They are smarter, kinder, and more capable.
I am at the bottom.
I have nothing to offer.
I will always be second-rate.

beliefs.belief: I'm helpless.
beliefs.origins: When a body or mind limits what we can do, tasks that were easy become hard and we depend on others. Over time, “I need help with some things” can become “I am helpless.
client_words: I cannot do anything.
I am useless.
I depend on everyone.
I have no power.
I am trapped.
I cannot help myself.

beliefs.belief: I'm less of a man (or woman) because of this.
beliefs.origins: Disability can challenge roles as provider, protector, caregiver, or athlete. Society’s images of strength can make us feel less masculine or feminine, especially when injury or illness changes how we work, parent, or relate.
client_words: I cannot be what I should be.
I have lost my role.
A real man (or woman) would not need this.
I am less than before.
I have failed my family.
I am not enough.

beliefs.belief: If I can't be independent, I have no dignity.
beliefs.origins: Needing help with dressing, bathing, eating, or finances can feel humiliating. A culture that prizes independence can make dependence seem shameful.
client_words: I am humiliated by needing help.
I have lost my dignity.
Being cared for makes me small.
I am a child again.
I hate being dependent.
I am diminished.

beliefs.belief: I'm always in the way.
beliefs.origins: Wheelchairs, walkers, slow movement, and special needs can make us feel obstructive in crowded places, in families, and in plans. Sighs, glances, and inaccessible spaces reinforce this.
client_words: I am a nuisance.
Everything has to change for me.
I slow everyone down.
I should stay home.
People wish I were not here.
I take up too much space.

beliefs.belief: People only feel sorry for me.
beliefs.origins: Pity can feel patronizing: a head tilt, extra helpfulness, lowered expectations. Over time, we may shut out all kindness to avoid being pitied.
client_words: They see me as a charity case.
They think I am pathetic.
Nobody respects me.
Kindness is just pity.
They do not see me.
I do not want sympathy.

beliefs.belief: I'm cut off from everyone.
beliefs.origins: Losing sight or hearing can make conversations tiring, gatherings confusing, and the world feel behind glass. Many withdraw to avoid the strain and embarrassment, and isolation grows.
client_words: I am in a bubble.
I cannot join in.
No one knows I am here.
It is too hard to connect.
I am alone with this.
The world has moved on without me.

beliefs.belief: People get tired of repeating things for me.
beliefs.origins: Asking “What?” again and again, or needing text or large print, can create guilt. Some nod along to avoid asking, and miss much.
client_words: I am annoying them.
They are tired of me.
I should stop asking.
I am a burden to talk to.
I will just pretend I heard.
They would rather not talk to me.

beliefs.belief: I can't enjoy life anymore.
beliefs.origins: When favorite pastimes like reading, music, conversation, or driving become hard or impossible, we mourn them. Without new sources of joy, life can seem gray.
client_words: Nothing is enjoyable anymore.
My favorite things are gone.
Life is dull.
I have lost joy.
There is nothing to look forward to.
I just exist.

beliefs.belief: I'll end up completely dependent on others.
beliefs.origins: Progressive vision or hearing loss raises a fear of losing independence completely. The fear can be worse than reality, and it can keep us from planning and using helpful tools.
client_words: I will lose all independence.
I will be a burden.
It will only get worse.
I will not be able to cope.
I will lose my home.
I will be helpless.

beliefs.belief: I'm embarrassing to be around.
beliefs.origins: Misheard answers, bumping into things, loud responses, and repeated requests can mortify us. We may fear that friends are ashamed to be seen with us.
client_words: They are ashamed of me.
I make things awkward.
People cringe when I talk.
I embarrass my family.
I should stay home.
Nobody wants me in public.

beliefs.belief: I'm ugly, so I'm unlovable.
beliefs.origins: Teasing, rejection, or constant exposure to idealized images can tie lovability to looks. After a few hurtful experiences, “I’m ugly” becomes “I’m unlovable.
client_words: No one could love me.
My face makes me unlovable.
I will be alone.
Beauty is necessary for love.
I am too ugly for anyone.
I do not deserve love.

beliefs.belief: My worth depends on how I look.
beliefs.origins: Constant evaluation of faces and bodies, by media, peers, and ourselves, can make appearance the basis of identity. Aging and change then threaten our worth itself.
client_words: I am my appearance.
If I look bad, I am worthless.
I need to look good to matter.
Aging will take my value.
I check mirrors constantly.
I cannot go out without makeup.

beliefs.belief: People are always staring and judging me.
beliefs.origins: Self-consciousness can make us feel watched, especially after trauma, bullying, or visible differences. Often others are absorbed in their own concerns, but the feeling of being watched is vivid.
client_words: Everyone is looking at me.
They are all judging.
I cannot go anywhere without being stared at.
I feel exposed.
I must hide.
They are talking about me.

beliefs.belief: No one could be attracted to me.
beliefs.origins: Rejection, comparisons, or scarring can make us believe romance is out of reach. We may avoid dating, friendships, or intimacy to avoid being hurt.
client_words: No one will ever want me.
I am not the type anyone falls for.
I will be alone forever.
I am not desirable.
Why bother dating?
People like me do not get loved.

beliefs.belief: If I looked different, my life would be fine.
beliefs.origins: It is tempting to believe that one change in our faces, weight, or skin would solve our troubles. The thought supports endless focus on appearance and delays dealing with deeper issues such as loneliness, grief, or fear.
client_words: Everything would be better if I looked better.
My problems are because of my looks.
I will be happy after I change.
People would like me if I looked right.
I would be confident.
This one thing holds me back.

beliefs.belief: I have to hide my difference to be accepted.
beliefs.origins: A birthmark, scar, limb difference, stutter, or other visible or hidden difference can lead to covering up, avoiding photos, or staying out of view. The effort is exhausting and can reinforce shame.
client_words: I must cover it.
If they see it, they will reject me.
I cannot be photographed.
I have to explain it.
I must keep it hidden.
My difference is shameful.

beliefs.belief: People see my difference before they see me.
beliefs.origins: First impressions are fast and often shaped by what is visible. Repeated experiences of being pigeonholed lead us to expect it always.
client_words: It is all they see.
I will always be defined by it.
They never see the real me.
First impressions are final.
I am a walking difference.
No one gets past it.

beliefs.belief: I'll always be the odd one out.
beliefs.origins: A lifetime of being the one who looks, moves, or sounds different can create the expectation that groups will never fully include us.
client_words: I never fit.
Everyone else matches.
I will always stand out.
I am the exception.
Groups will always push me out.
I will never belong.

beliefs.belief: I'll never fit in.
beliefs.origins: Repeated experiences of exclusion or teasing create a lasting expectation that fitting in is impossible. We may stop trying or adopt a defensive stance.
client_words: No group will take me.
I am not like others.
I will always be outside.
Trying is pointless.
I do not have what it takes.
I am too different.

beliefs.belief: Something is wrong with me because I don't look like others.
beliefs.origins: Difference is often treated as deficiency, by media, peers, and sometimes medical language. Children especially take this in as fact about themselves.
client_words: I am wrong.
Normal looks are right.
I was made badly.
I am a mistake.
There must be something wrong with me.
I do not belong in the human family.

beliefs.belief: God is punishing me with this illness.
beliefs.origins: Many have heard that sickness is God’s punishment, or they search their past for what they did wrong. Guilt over past sins can attach itself to a diagnosis.
client_words: I deserve this.
God is angry at me.
This is payback.
I must have sinned.
God is teaching me a lesson.
My past caught up with me.

beliefs.belief: I must have done something to deserve this.
beliefs.origins: The mind seeks explanations for pain, and self-blame can feel easier than randomness. Rumination about past mistakes fuels shame.
client_words: It is my fault.
If I had been better, this would not have happened.
This is what I get.
I deserve to suffer.
I brought it on myself.
God is balancing the scales.

beliefs.belief: A loving God wouldn't let me suffer like this.
beliefs.origins: Pain makes God’s love hard to see. If He is all-powerful and loving, the logic seems to say He would stop it.
client_words: If God loved me, He would stop it.
He could help but does not.
Love would not let this happen.
Either He is not loving or not powerful.
God has turned away.
I do not understand His love.

beliefs.belief: God has abandoned me.
beliefs.origins: In long illness, prayers can feel unanswered and God silent. Loneliness and pain make His presence hard to sense.
client_words: God has left me.
He is silent because He is gone.
I am on my own.
He does not care.
My prayers go nowhere.
I feel nothing.

beliefs.belief: My suffering is meaningless.
beliefs.origins: Pain without explanation can feel pointless, and nothing seems to come from it. The inability to see any good makes it worse.
client_words: It is all for nothing.
There is no point.
I get nothing out of this.
God wastes my pain.
No good will come.
It is senseless.

beliefs.belief: If I had enough faith, God would heal me.
beliefs.origins: Some teachers and friends say that healing depends on the size of our faith. When healing does not come, guilt and doubt pile on top of illness.
client_words: My faith is too small.
God is waiting for me to believe more.
It is my fault I am not healed.
Real faith always heals.
I am blocking my own healing.
I must try harder.

beliefs.belief: God doesn't hear my prayers, or He would have taken this away.
beliefs.origins: After praying for months or years for relief, silence can feel like rejection. Some conclude that God is not listening or does not care.
client_words: God ignores me.
My prayers bounce off the ceiling.
He answers others, not me.
He could heal me if He wanted.
Prayer is pointless.
God does not care.

beliefs.belief: Needing medication means my faith is weak.
beliefs.origins: Some believers are taught that faith and medicine are opposed. Taking pills can then feel like a lack of trust.
client_words: A strong believer would trust God alone.
Medicine shows I doubt God.
I am cheating on faith.
If God is my healer, I should not need pills.
Others are healed by faith alone.
I feel guilty taking it.

beliefs.belief: Christians shouldn't get depressed or anxious.
beliefs.origins: Many churches speak of joy and peace without space for struggle. Believers who feel depressed or anxious may think they are failing, or that they are not truly saved.
client_words: Real Christians are always joyful.
I am failing God.
I should be able to pray this away.
My faith must be weak.
I should not need help.
Others will think less of me.

beliefs.belief: If I'm not healed, I must not be right with God.
beliefs.origins: Some equate health with God’s favor and illness with distance from Him. Without healing, we may scour our lives for hidden sin or doubt our salvation.
client_words: Healthy people are in good standing with God.
I am being passed over.
I am out of favor.
Something is blocking me.
I should be healed if I were right.
I am under a cloud.

beliefs.belief: God can't use me in this condition.
beliefs.origins: Illness can erase roles in ministry, work, and family. When we cannot do what we used to do, we may feel set aside by God.
client_words: I am too limited.
God needs strong people.
I have been set aside.
I can’t do what I used to.
My usefulness is over.
There is nothing I can offer.

beliefs.belief: I'm useless to the church now.
beliefs.origins: When we cannot attend, teach, serve, or give as before, we may feel invisible to the church. Sometimes churches fail to include those who are limited.
client_words: The church does not need me.
I contribute nothing.
They have forgotten me.
I am a burden to the church.
I used to be useful.
Only active people matter.

beliefs.belief: My limitations disqualify me from God's purpose.
beliefs.origins: We often equate purpose with achievement. When limitations constrain what we do, it seems that God’s purposes have passed us by.
client_words: My purpose is lost.
I am out of the picture.
God’s plan needs strong people.
I cannot fulfill my calling.
I am disqualified.
Limits end purpose.

beliefs.belief: I have nothing left to give.
beliefs.origins: Long illness, caregiving, or chronic fatigue can leave us depleted. With no energy to give, we may feel empty and ashamed.
client_words: I am empty.
I cannot help anyone.
I have no energy.
I am a taker.
I have nothing to offer.
Everyone gives more than I do.

beliefs.belief: Only healthy, strong people can serve God well.
beliefs.origins: Church culture often celebrates energetic, visible service. Those with chronic illness or limits may feel their service is inferior or unseen.
client_words: Only the strong can serve.
My service does not count.
I am a spectator.
God prefers healthy workers.
My weakness hinders God.
Visible service matters more.

beliefs.belief: I can't let my guard down
beliefs.origins: Feeling betrayed, bullied, deceived, or mistreated can result in a person being more or less constantly alert and anxious. You may find you spend a great deal of your time scanning your environment, looking out for possible threats.
client_words: People always have a hidden agenda.
If someone is kind, they probably want something.
I must watch for every sign of betrayal.
If I relax, I will miss the danger.
I cannot tell anyone what I really think.
Depending on someone gives them power to hurt me.

beliefs.belief: Friendliness usually hides an ulterior motive.
beliefs.origins: Past manipulation, broken promises, betrayal, or inconsistent care may teach a person to question friendly behavior. These experiences can make caution understandable.
client_words: They're being nice because they want something.
No one is friendly without a reason.
A compliment is probably a trap.
If I accept help, I'll owe them.
I need to figure out what they really want.
People only pretend to care.

beliefs.belief: I need to hide the real me in order to not get hurt.
beliefs.origins: If honesty was met with ridicule, rejection, punishment, or betrayal, hiding may once have felt protective. A person may learn to show only a polished version of themselves.
client_words: If people really knew me, they would use it against me.
I must look strong and keep my struggles hidden.
My honest feelings will drive people away.
It is safer to be what others expect.
I should say I am fine even when I need support.
Being known means losing control.

beliefs.belief: People always try to hide what they are doing
beliefs.origins: Believing that you have been deceived, betrayed, or surprised by someone’s harmful actions can teach you to expect that they are communicating hidden plans or meanings. Family secrecy, unpredictable behavior, or repeated warnings about other people can strengthen the belief that you must always search beneath the…
client_words: They are keeping something from me.
If I stop watching, they will catch me off guard.
There must be another reason they are doing this.
I need to work out what they are really planning.
A vague answer means they are deceiving me.
I cannot relax until I know their true intentions.

beliefs.belief: Little things often have great significance
beliefs.origins: When small details once preceded criticism, conflict, or disappointment, you may have learned to watch them closely. Repeated warnings, perfectionistic expectations, or stressful experiences can also teach you that little mistakes have major consequences.
client_words: That small comment must mean something serious.
One mistake changes everything.
If I ignore this detail, I will regret it.
This little setback shows that everything is going wrong.
I need to keep thinking about it until I know its full meaning.
The fact that I noticed it means it must be important.

beliefs.belief: Avoiding people and new challenges is safer than risking embarrassment.
beliefs.origins: Repeated criticism, teasing, shaming, or being left out can teach a person that other people are a source of pain. A child who was often corrected harshly, compared with others, or humiliated may learn that staying quiet and out of view is the best way to stay safe.
client_words: It is safer to stay home than to risk looking foolish.
I will pass on that job or event; I would only embarrass myself.
If I never try, I can never fail in front of anyone.
I will wait until I feel confident before I join in.
I would rather be alone than be judged.
Why take the chance when I already know how it will go?

beliefs.belief: I am inadequate and less than other people.
beliefs.origins: Harsh criticism, constant comparison with a sibling or classmate, being rejected, or growing up without encouragement can plant the idea that we are not enough. A child cannot easily separate “what happened to me” from “who I am,” so the feeling can settle in as a belief about identity.
client_words: Everyone else seems to have it together except me.
I am not as smart, interesting, or capable as other people.
I do not belong here.
Other people are simply better than I am.
I will never measure up.
If they only knew how ordinary I am, they would lose interest.

beliefs.belief: I am awkward and unlikable, and I have little to offer.
beliefs.origins: Being teased, ignored, or told “you’re too quiet” or “you’re too much” can teach a person to distrust their own personality. Shyness or a few awkward moments can be remembered vividly and turned into a verdict.
client_words: I never know what to say.
I am boring.
People are just being polite when they talk to me.
There is something wrong with my personality.
I have nothing interesting to add.
I am not the kind of person people want to be around.

beliefs.belief: I must be sure people will like me before I let them know me.
beliefs.origins: A person who was loved only when they performed well, or who was hurt after being open, may learn that acceptance must be earned first. Sharing something personal and being laughed at, or being betrayed, can lead to a rule: “Do not show myself until I know it is safe.
client_words: I will join in when I am sure they like me.
I should not open up until I know it is safe.
If I show who I am, they will leave.
I have to be liked first.
I cannot risk it without a guarantee.
It is better to keep my distance than to be rejected.

beliefs.belief: Ridicule or criticism would prove I am worthless, and I could not bear it.
beliefs.origins: A person who was shamed in front of others, ridiculed at home or school, or humiliated for mistakes may come to dread it above almost anything. Early shaming can leave a lasting sense that exposure equals disgrace, so even mild criticism can feel like a blow to the whole self.
client_words: If they laugh at me, I will be crushed.
One criticism proves what I have always feared about myself.
I could not stand being humiliated.
Being embarrassed would be the worst thing.
If I fail in front of people, I will never recover.
Criticism means I am worthless.

beliefs.belief: Getting close to people will cost me my freedom.
beliefs.origins: A person who grew up with controlling, intrusive, or unpredictable caregivers may learn that being close means being managed, criticized, or swallowed up. Others learned that needs were a burden and that self-reliance was the safe way to live.
client_words: If I let someone in, they will take over my life.
I need my space, and people always want more of me.
Being close means giving up who I am.
I stay free by not getting involved.
Commitments are cages.
It is easier to keep everyone at a distance.

beliefs.belief: I don’t need anyone. I am better off alone.
beliefs.origins: A child whose needs went unmet, or who learned that people were unreliable, can decide to need no one. Being self-sufficient then becomes a source of pride and safety.
client_words: I do not need anyone.
I am happier on my own.
People just complicate things.
I have always been a loner, and that is fine.
I can handle everything myself.
Other people are not worth the trouble.

beliefs.belief: Depending on anyone only leads to trouble.
beliefs.origins: When people who should have been dependable were absent, unpredictable, or let us down, we learn that depending on others ends in disappointment. A child who had to take care of herself or himself too early can decide that needing anyone is dangerous.
client_words: If I rely on someone, they will let me down.
It is safer to do everything myself.
Needing people just creates problems.
I do not ask for help.
People are only reliable until they are not.
I would rather struggle alone than owe anyone.

beliefs.belief: My feelings aren’t worth sharing. Talking about them changes nothing.
beliefs.origins: When feelings were ignored, dismissed, or ridiculed in childhood, a person can learn that they do not matter and that talking about them makes no difference. In some families, feelings simply were not talked about.
client_words: No one wants to hear how I feel.
Talking about it will not help.
My feelings are not important.
I would just be a burden.
It is easier to keep everything inside.
Why bother saying it? Nothing will change.

beliefs.belief: Relationships take more than they give, so they aren’t worth the effort.
beliefs.origins: Someone who grew up caring for others, or in a home where closeness meant constant demands and little warmth, may learn that people take far more than they give. If the benefits of friendship were rarely experienced, the cost is all that is remembered.
client_words: People are exhausting.
I give and give and get nothing back.
It is not worth the energy.
I have better things to do than keep up friendships.
Relationships are more work than they are worth.
I am better off with fewer demands.

beliefs.belief: What other people think of me doesn’t matter.
beliefs.origins: Some people learn early that other people’s opinions were unreliable, harsh, or impossible to please, so they decide to stop caring. Others have been hurt so often by criticism that indifference feels safer than hope.
client_words: I do not care what anyone thinks.
Praise and criticism mean nothing to me.
Their opinions are irrelevant.
I set my own standards.
No one’s view of me affects me.
I do not need anyone’s approval or advice.

beliefs.belief: I’ve given up on letting people in.
beliefs.origins: Long seasons of disappointment, rejection, or loss can lead a person to quit trying. The shield that was once raised for protection becomes permanent, and the person may even feel relief at no longer hoping.
client_words: I am done trying.
It never works out.
I have shut that part of me off.
I would rather not hope.
Nothing will change.
I do not feel anything anymore.

beliefs.belief: Close relationships aren’t important to me.
beliefs.origins: When earlier closeness brought pain, demands, or disappointment, a person may decide that intimacy is not worth the cost. Others genuinely feel little pull toward people, and over time they conclude that relationships do not matter.
client_words: Intimacy is not important to me.
I do not need anyone close.
Relationships are not worth the effort.
I am fine without a close connection.
I am simply not a relational person.
Others make too much of closeness.

beliefs.belief: I shouldn’t confide in anyone.
beliefs.origins: A confidence that was betrayed, a childhood where private things were mocked or used against us, or a home where feelings were not welcome can teach us that keeping things to ourselves is the only safe way. Privacy is a healthy value.
client_words: It is safer to keep things to myself.
Nobody can be trusted with my secrets.
Sharing only makes things worse.
I should handle my own business.
What I say will be used against me.
Privacy is the only protection.

beliefs.belief: Nothing is much fun anyway, so I might as well be on my own.
beliefs.origins: Sometimes the capacity for enjoyment fades. This can follow long stress, loss, depression, or years of keeping people at a distance, and sometimes a person has simply always been somewhat quiet and low-key.
client_words: Nothing is fun anymore.
I do not enjoy anything.
Why bother going out?
I am happier on my own.
Social events are a waste of time.
I do not feel much of anything.

beliefs.topic: Intense Emotions and Fear of Abandonment
beliefs.belief: The people I love will eventually leave me.
beliefs.origins: This fear often grows out of real loss: a parent who left or was emotionally absent, a divorce, a death, a betrayal, or a friend who disappeared. When people we needed did leave, the mind learns to expect it.
client_words: They are going to leave.
Everyone leaves in the end.
I cannot count on anyone to stay.
It is only a matter of time.
If I get close, I will be hurt.
They are pulling away.

beliefs.topic: Intense Emotions and Fear of Abandonment
beliefs.belief: If people really knew me, they would not accept me.
beliefs.origins: This belief often grows where love felt conditional: where mistakes brought anger or silence, where a person had to earn approval, or where feelings were dismissed. A child in that setting learns that the real self is a problem and a performed self is safer.
client_words: If they knew the real me, they would leave.
I have to be careful what I show.
I do not even know who I am.
Something is wrong with me.
I am too much, or not enough.
I am only liked when I perform.

beliefs.topic: Intense Emotions and Fear of Abandonment
beliefs.belief: I can’t manage life without someone to lean on.
beliefs.origins: Some people never had the chance to learn they could cope. A parent who did everything, or a parent who was unreliable and left them anxious, can leave a person doubting their own ability.
client_words: I cannot do this on my own.
I would fall apart without them.
I need someone with me.
I am helpless alone.
I do not know how to handle things.
I cannot be left on my own.

beliefs.topic: Intense Emotions and Fear of Abandonment
beliefs.belief: My feelings are so strong they will completely overwhelm me.
beliefs.origins: Some people are born more emotionally sensitive, and others grew up where feelings were ignored, punished, or unpredictable, so they never learned how to settle them. When emotions feel enormous and nobody showed a way through, it is natural to fear them.
client_words: I cannot stand this feeling.
It is too much.
I am going to fall apart.
I will lose control.
This will never stop.
I have to do something right now.

beliefs.topic: Intense Emotions and Fear of Abandonment
beliefs.belief: Any disagreement means the people I love are about to reject me.
beliefs.origins: In some homes a disagreement led to coldness, rage, or someone leaving, so conflict came to signal danger. A person may also tend to see people as all good or all bad, so when someone they love does something upsetting, it can feel as if that person has turned against them.
client_words: They are angry, so they are leaving.
We disagreed, so it is over.
I must have ruined everything.
They do not really care about me.
I have to fix this right now.
I should just agree.

beliefs.belief: Using other people is necessary to get by.
beliefs.origins: People who grew up where needs went unmet, where adults could not be trusted, or where only the strong did well often conclude that survival means getting what you can from others before they get it from you. For a time this view may have even protected you.
client_words: Nobody looks out for me but me.
Everyone is out for themselves.
If I do not use them, they will use me.
People are there to be used.
Only suckers play fair.
I do what I have to do.

beliefs.belief: What I want matters more than other people’s rights.
beliefs.origins: A child who was indulged without limits, or who learned that taking was the only way to get anything, can grow up treating wants as rights. Others learned this in homes where the strongest got their way.
client_words: I deserve what I want.
Why should I wait?
Their problem is not mine.
Rules are for other people.
If I want it, I should have it.
Nobody should stand in my way.

beliefs.belief: Bending the truth is fine when it helps me.
beliefs.origins: Some people learned early that honesty brought punishment, so they learned to say whatever kept them safe. Others grew up around people who lied freely and rewarded cleverness.
client_words: A little lie never hurt anyone.
Everyone shades the truth.
I had to say that to get out of it.
They did not need to know.
I can talk my way out of anything.
Honesty is for people who can afford it.

beliefs.belief: Staying in control keeps me from being controlled.
beliefs.origins: Many people who hold this belief were once controlled themselves by a harsh parent, an abusive partner, or a rough environment. The lesson they took was never to be the weak one again.
client_words: If I do not take charge, someone else will.
I will never be pushed around again.
Respect means fear.
Giving in is weakness.
I have to win.
People only listen to force.

beliefs.belief: If I’ve been wronged, I have the right to get even.
beliefs.origins: Many who think this way have really been wronged, sometimes badly, and nobody made it right. When justice never came, taking matters into your own hands can seem the only fair response.
client_words: They had it coming.
I will not let this go.
Somebody has to pay.
If I do not hit back, I look weak.
It is only fair.
No one will protect me but me.

beliefs.belief: I am fundamentally unlike other people.
Ordinary coincidences carry personal messages.
My thoughts can cause unrelated events.
Unusual sensations confirm my unusual explanations.
Other people’s intentions are usually threatening.
Attention determines my worth.
I must entertain people to retain affection.
Being unnoticed means being insignificant.
Stronger displays are necessary to be heard.
My feelings reliably establish what is true.
I am entitled to exceptional treatment.
Ordinary limits should not apply to me.
Admiration establishes my importance.
Criticism is an unacceptable humiliation.
Other people should prioritize my needs.
I lack the ability to cope independently.
Other people’s judgment is better than mine.
Disagreement threatens the support I need.
Keeping support requires surrendering my preferences.
Being alone means being helpless.
Only flawless performance is acceptable.
Mistakes signal personal failure.
Strict control prevents disaster.
Delegating means accepting unacceptable risks.
My standards should govern everyone’s behavior.
My parents never loved me.
beliefs.origins: Some of us grew up with parents who were distant, harsh, absent, addicted, or simply unable to show love in a way we could feel. Children draw their conclusions from what they experience, and a child who did not feel loved often decides, “I was unlovable,” or “they never loved me.” That conclusion can then shape…
client_words: I was never wanted.
There must be something wrong with me or they would have loved me.
No one will ever love me the way a parent should.
I do not matter to the people who should care most.
Love is for other people.
I will always feel unloved.

beliefs.belief: I can never please my parents.
beliefs.origins: Some parents set standards that keep moving. A good grade is met with “why not an A-plus,” a success is met with silence, and a mistake is remembered for years.
client_words: Nothing I do is ever enough.
They will always find something wrong.
I am a disappointment to them.
If I try harder, maybe they will finally approve.
I dread seeing them.
I cannot relax around them.

beliefs.belief: What my parents said about me must be true.
beliefs.origins: Children believe what their parents say. If we were told we were lazy, stupid, selfish, ugly, or “just like” a difficult relative, those words went in deeply, and we may still repeat them to ourselves.
client_words: They said I was worthless, so I must be.
They know me best.
I will always be the stupid one.
I am exactly what they said I was.
I cannot trust my own opinion of myself.
If it was said so often, it must be true.

beliefs.belief: I have to earn my parents' love.
beliefs.origins: Where affection was given for achievement and withdrawn for failure, children learn that love is a wage. Praise for grades, sports, or good behavior, and coldness for mistakes, teach that we are loved for what we do.
client_words: If I stop achieving, they will stop caring.
Love is something I have to deserve.
I have to keep proving myself.
When I fail, I lose their love.
I must make them proud.
Their love is always one mistake away.

beliefs.belief: I can't be happy until my parents change.
beliefs.origins: When parents have hurt us, we may wait for an apology or a change that never comes. Holiday after holiday, we hope this will be the time they finally see us, and each disappointment reopens the wound.
client_words: I will never be at peace until they apologize.
As long as they act this way, I cannot be happy.
They ruined my life.
My happiness depends on their changing.
I cannot move on until they admit what they did.
I am stuck until they change.

beliefs.belief: I'm a failure as a parent.
beliefs.origins: Parenting is the one job where we are graded daily and never fully trained. Comparison with other parents, a child’s struggles, our own childhood wounds, and criticism from relatives or church can leave us convinced that we are failing.
client_words: Good parents do not make these mistakes.
Everyone else is doing better than I am.
I yelled again, so I am a terrible parent.
My child deserves better.
I do not know what I am doing.
I am failing them.

beliefs.belief: If my child struggles, it's my fault.
beliefs.origins: Parents often feel responsible for everything that happens to their children. When a child struggles with anxiety, school, friends, behavior, or faith, we search our own parenting for the cause.
client_words: I must have caused this.
If I had been a better parent, they would not struggle.
It is all because of what I did.
I should have seen this coming.
Other parents’ kids are fine.
It is my job to fix everything.

beliefs.belief: I have ruined my children.
beliefs.origins: Looking back on yelling, divorce, absence, addiction, neglect, or hard years, some parents decide the damage is permanent. Guilt can be especially heavy when a child is hurting now and we can see the connection.
client_words: The damage is permanent.
They will never forgive me.
I cannot undo what I did.
My children are hurt because of me.
It is too late to make it right.
I destroyed their childhood.

beliefs.belief: I'm turning into my own parents.
beliefs.origins: Many of us hear our parent’s words come out of our own mouths and feel a chill. If we grew up with anger, coldness, addiction, or control, we may fear that we are destined to repeat it.
client_words: I am becoming exactly what I swore I would not.
It is in my blood.
I cannot help it.
My children will end up like me.
I never had a good model.
I will repeat the same cycle.

beliefs.belief: It's too late to be a good parent to my kids.
beliefs.origins: Parents of teenagers and adult children often feel the window has closed. Years of absence, anger, addiction, or distraction cannot be taken back.
client_words: They are grown and the damage is done.
They do not need me now.
I missed my chance.
Nothing I say will matter.
They will never want a relationship with me.
I should have changed years ago.

beliefs.belief: My family will never change.
beliefs.origins: Family patterns can feel carved in stone: the same arguments, the same favorites, the same silence about hard things. After years of hoping and trying, it is natural to conclude that nothing will ever be different.
client_words: They are who they are.
Nothing I do makes any difference.
Every holiday is the same.
They will never see the truth.
It is pointless to try again.
I have to accept it forever.

beliefs.belief: I have to keep everyone in my family happy.
beliefs.origins: Some of us became the family peacekeeper early, learning to read moods and smooth things over before anyone exploded. We may have been rewarded for it or been afraid not to.
client_words: If someone is upset, I must have done something.
I cannot say no without causing a blowup.
I have to make sure everyone has a good time.
It is my job to keep the peace.
I cannot relax until everyone is okay.
Their moods are my responsibility.

beliefs.belief: I'm the black sheep, and I'll never belong.
beliefs.origins: In many families, one person ends up as the odd one out: the one who thinks differently, left the faith, made a different choice, or was blamed for the family’s problems. Years of being misunderstood, teased, or excluded can harden into the belief that we will never belong anywhere.
client_words: I will always be the outsider.
They never understood me.
There is something wrong with me.
I do not belong in any family.
I am the problem.
Nobody will ever make room for me.

beliefs.belief: Family means I must put up with anything.
beliefs.origins: Family loyalty is a gift, but it can be bent into a trap. Some of us were taught that family comes first no matter what, that we should never speak about problems outside the home, or that forgiving means staying in harm’s way.
client_words: Family always comes first, no matter what.
I cannot say anything about how they treat me.
Good family members take it.
If I set limits, I am betraying them.
What happens at home stays at home.
They are my family, so I have to endure it.

beliefs.belief: I'm responsible for fixing my family's problems.
beliefs.origins: In many families one person becomes the fixer: the capable one who steps in with money, advice, rescues, or mediation. Often it begins in childhood, when a parent was overwhelmed.
client_words: If I do not step in, everything will fall apart.
They need me to fix this.
I am the only responsible one.
It is my fault if they struggle.
I cannot rest until it is solved.
Who else will do it?

beliefs.belief: Nobody really likes me.
beliefs.origins: Being left out, teased, or ignored, especially in childhood or adolescence, can plant the idea that we are unlikable. A few painful experiences can become a lens: a friend who does not text back means dislike, a quiet group means rejection.
client_words: People only tolerate me.
If I disappeared, nobody would notice.
Everyone finds me boring or annoying.
They are being nice out of pity.
I will always be on the outside.
There is something unlikable about me.

beliefs.belief: I don't fit in anywhere.
beliefs.origins: Some of us were always a little different: in family, school, church, or work. Moves, culture, temperament, or interests can leave us feeling like the one who never quite matches the room.
client_words: I never match the people around me.
I always feel out of place.
There is no group for someone like me.
I have to change who I am to be accepted.
I will always be the odd one.
Everyone else seems to know the rules.

beliefs.belief: If people really knew me, they would leave.
beliefs.origins: If we have been rejected after being honest, shamed for a mistake, or teased for being vulnerable, we learn to hide. We show a polished version and keep the rest locked away.
client_words: If they saw the real me, they would be disgusted.
I have to keep my guard up.
My past would scare them off.
They like me only because they do not know me.
No one could love all of me.
I must never let anyone see my weaknesses.

beliefs.belief: Everyone else has real friends but me.
beliefs.origins: Social media, church directories, and group photos make it look as if everyone else has a full circle of close friends. Life changes such as moves, marriage, parenting, job changes, and illness can thin out friendships.
client_words: Everyone else has a best friend.
I am the only one who has no one.
I missed the window for making friends.
Other people connect so easily.
I will always be alone.
No one calls me.

beliefs.belief: I have to be useful to be wanted.
beliefs.origins: Some of us learned that we were welcome when we helped: when we cooked, listened, fixed, drove, or gave. If affection came mostly when we were useful, we learned that our value was our usefulness.
client_words: If I stop helping, they will drop me.
I must earn my place.
I am only wanted when I am needed.
I cannot just be a guest.
My value is in what I give.
If I say no, I will be left out.

beliefs.belief: Christians will judge me.
beliefs.origins: Many people have experienced a cold look, a gossip circle, or a sermon that felt like a finger pointing at them. Some of us were judged for divorce, doubt, addiction, appearance, or politics.
client_words: They will look down on me.
Church people are hypocrites.
If they knew, they would condemn me.
I will be talked about.
I do not meet their standards.
It is safer to stay away.

beliefs.belief: Everyone at church has it all together but me.
beliefs.origins: On Sunday morning people arrive in nice clothes, smiling, with children in order and answers ready. We see their best and compare it with our worst.
client_words: They have no problems.
I am the only one who is struggling.
Everyone else is more spiritual.
If I show my struggles, I will not belong.
I must be failing as a Christian.
Their lives are perfect.

beliefs.belief: Because church people hurt me, God must be just like them.
beliefs.origins: When those who speak for God use that voice to control, shame, or harm, it is hard to separate them from God. A pastor’s betrayal, a youth leader’s abuse of trust, or a church’s harsh rejection can leave a child or adult convinced that God shares their coldness or cruelty.
client_words: If that is what Christians are like, I want nothing to do with God.
God let them do it, so He must be like them.
They spoke for God, so God must agree with them.
I cannot trust God after that.
All religion is just control.
God is as harsh as they were.

beliefs.belief: I don't belong in church because of my past.
beliefs.origins: A history of addiction, divorce, abortion, prison, affairs, or years away from God can make a church building feel like a courtroom. We imagine that everyone has a spotless record and that our past would be unwelcome.
client_words: People like me do not belong.
If they knew my past, they would ask me to leave.
I have been too far away for too long.
I am too damaged.
I will bring shame on the church.
I need to clean up first.

beliefs.belief: I have to hide my struggles from other Christians.
beliefs.origins: If we have seen others gossiped about, or if our church culture praises victory and quiets doubt, we learn to say “I’m fine.” We fear that sharing a struggle with anxiety, marriage, money, or temptation will cost us respect or leadership. So we smile, pray alone, and hurt in secret.
client_words: If I tell, they will think less of me.
Strong Christians do not struggle.
I have to keep it together.
They will gossip.
I have to handle this alone.
Sharing will cost me my position.

beliefs.belief: My boss will always find fault with me.
beliefs.origins: A critical parent, teacher, or earlier boss can train us to scan every authority figure for disapproval. At work, a brief tone or a correction can feel like proof that we are in trouble.
client_words: No matter what I do, they will criticize me.
Every email from my boss is a warning.
I am always one mistake from trouble.
They have it in for me.
I cannot do anything right.
I dread every meeting.

beliefs.belief: I have to be perfect or I'll lose my job.
beliefs.origins: Perfectionism at work often starts in childhood, where mistakes were punished or achievement was praised. A real workplace layoff, a harsh review, or a close call can cement it.
client_words: One mistake and I am out.
I cannot afford any errors.
Everyone else is flawless.
I must work twice as hard.
I will be found out.
Perfect or nothing.

beliefs.belief: People in authority can't be trusted.
beliefs.origins: If a parent, teacher, coach, pastor, or boss abused or betrayed authority, the lesson may stay: authority means danger. We may bristle at supervision, expect to be used, or avoid anyone who has power over us.
client_words: Anyone with power will misuse it.
They will use me and then drop me.
I cannot rely on bosses or leaders.
If I submit, I will be hurt.
I have to protect myself from them.
Authority is dangerous.

beliefs.belief: I'll never be respected at work.
beliefs.origins: Being overlooked, interrupted, or passed over, or being the youngest, newest, or quietest person in a room, can leave us feeling invisible. A history of being dismissed at home or school makes it easier to read workplace slights as permanent verdicts.
client_words: No one takes me seriously.
They talk over me.
I am invisible here.
I will always be the junior one.
My ideas do not count.
They will never see my value.

beliefs.belief: If I speak up, I'll be punished.
beliefs.origins: Speaking up has cost some people dearly: in families where disagreement brought anger, at schools or churches where questions were treated as rebellion, or at workplaces where complaints led to retaliation. We learn to stay quiet, swallow concerns, and agree on the surface.
client_words: If I say anything, I will pay for it.
It is safer to stay quiet.
They will retaliate.
No one wants to hear what I think.
I will lose my job or the relationship.
Speaking up never works.

beliefs.belief: No one will ever want me.
beliefs.origins: Rejection in dating, a breakup, or years of watching friends pair off can feel like a final judgment. Earlier messages about looks, weight, family, or worth can make every unreturned message sound like confirmation.
client_words: I am unattractive and unlovable.
Everyone else finds someone but me.
Nobody has ever really wanted me.
I will end up alone.
I do not have anything to offer.
The next rejection will prove it.

beliefs.belief: I'm single because something is wrong with me.
beliefs.origins: In a culture and sometimes a church that treats marriage as the normal goal, a single adult can feel like a puzzle others are trying to solve. Well-meaning questions, such as “Why aren’t you married yet?” can leave us scanning ourselves for defects.
client_words: There must be a reason no one chose me.
I am too much, or not enough.
Everyone else sees my flaws.
If I fix myself, I will find someone.
Something about me pushes people away.
I am defective.

beliefs.belief: I'm too old to find love.
beliefs.origins: Birthdays can feel like a closing door. A culture that celebrates youth, a divorce or widowhood in later years, or a long season of waiting can convince us that love is for the young.
client_words: That ship has sailed.
No one wants someone my age.
All the good ones are taken.
I missed my chance.
It is too late to start over.
Love is for younger people.

beliefs.belief: I need a partner to be complete.
beliefs.origins: Songs, movies, and even sermons can suggest that one is half a person until paired up. After a breakup or in a long single season, loneliness can feel like proof.
client_words: I am only half a person alone.
I will not be happy until I have someone.
I cannot cope on my own.
A partner would fix my emptiness.
Being single is a lesser life.
I need someone to be whole.

beliefs.belief: God is keeping me single because he is displeased with me.
beliefs.origins: When we pray for a partner and nothing happens, it is tempting to wonder whether God is withholding it. If we carry guilt over our past, it is easy to link the two.
client_words: God is holding out on me.
He is punishing me for my past.
I did not pray right.
He gives spouses to people who are better than me.
I am being tested and failing.
God must be angry with me.

beliefs.belief: I'll never be able to trust anyone again.
beliefs.origins: After betrayal by a spouse, friend, parent, or church, trust feels dangerous. We learn to scan for signs, hold back, and avoid vulnerability.
client_words: I will never let anyone close again.
Everyone will let me down.
It is safer to rely only on myself.
I cannot read people anymore.
I was a fool to trust.
I will always expect the worst.

beliefs.belief: Because my marriage ended, I'm a failure.
beliefs.origins: Divorce comes with shame, whether we initiated it or not. We may feel judged by family or church, and haunted by what we could have done.
client_words: I failed at the most important commitment.
I am a failure as a spouse.
I should have tried harder.
God cannot use me now.
People see me as a failure.
I wasted years.

beliefs.belief: If I had been better, they would not have left.
beliefs.origins: When someone leaves a marriage, a friendship, or a family, we look for the reason, and we often settle on ourselves because that gives us a sense of control. If only I had been more attractive, more patient, more successful, then they would have stayed.
client_words: It is my fault they left.
If I had changed, they would be here.
I drove them away.
I was not good enough.
I should have done more.
Everything would be different if I were different.

beliefs.belief: Everyone I love eventually betrays me.
beliefs.origins: Repeated hurt by parents, partners, friends, or church can form a pattern: love ends in betrayal. We may expect it, pull away early, or test people until they fail.
client_words: Everyone leaves in the end.
Love always ends in betrayal.
I should expect it.
I will be hurt again.
It is only a matter of time.
I cannot count on anyone.

beliefs.belief: I'm damaged goods.
beliefs.origins: After divorce, abuse, a sexual past, repeated rejection, or being used, many people feel permanently marked. The phrase “damaged goods” may have been said to us, or we may say it ourselves.
client_words: No one wants someone with my history.
I am used and worthless.
I am permanently broken.
I have less to offer than other people.
My past has ruined me.
I do not deserve a good relationship.

beliefs.belief: I'll never get over losing them.
beliefs.origins: Grief can feel endless, especially in the first year or after a sudden or traumatic loss. Well-meaning people may say “time heals” or “you should be over this,” and when it does not feel true, we conclude that something is wrong with us or that the pain is permanent.
client_words: The pain will never lessen.
I will always feel like this.
I cannot go on without them.
Life will never be good again.
Something is wrong with me for still hurting.
I will never be happy again.

beliefs.belief: If I had done something different, they would still be alive.
beliefs.origins: After a death, the mind searches for what could have been done: a symptom missed, a call not made, a different route, a different decision. This is a normal part of grief, because the alternative, that we could not control it, is frightening.
client_words: I should have noticed.
If only I had called sooner.
It is my fault.
I let them die.
I could have prevented it.
I will never forgive myself.

beliefs.belief: Moving on means forgetting them.
beliefs.origins: Many grieving people fear that feeling better is a betrayal. If we laugh, enjoy a meal, or begin to plan ahead, it can feel like leaving the person behind.
client_words: If I smile, I am betraying them.
If I stop hurting, it means I did not love them.
I must keep suffering to honor them.
I do not deserve to be happy.
Moving on is disloyal.
I will forget their voice and face.

beliefs.belief: God took them from me to punish me.
beliefs.origins: After a death, guilt over old sins or an unresolved conflict can lead us to wonder if God is repaying us. People of faith can add to this by saying things like “God needed another angel” or “everything happens for a reason,” which can make God sound like the cause of the loss and imply that we deserved it.
client_words: I am being punished for my sin.
God took them because of what I did.
I deserved to lose them.
God is angry with me.
If I had been better, they would be here.
This is the price of my past.

beliefs.belief: Grieving shows a lack of faith.
beliefs.origins: Some Christians are told to “be strong,” “rejoice, they are in a better place,” or “don’t cry.” Those words may come from love, but they can leave mourners feeling that tears are a spiritual failure. We then grieve privately or pretend to be fine.
client_words: Strong believers do not cry this much.
If I really trusted God, I would be at peace.
My tears show I doubt.
I should be rejoicing, not mourning.
People will think my faith is weak.
I am letting God down.

beliefs.belief: If I forgive them, I'm saying what they did was okay.
beliefs.origins: We often resist forgiveness because we fear it erases the wrong. If someone hurt us badly, forgiving can feel like letting them off the hook, minimizing our pain, or telling the world that their behavior is acceptable.
client_words: Forgiving them means it did not matter.
If I forgive, they win.
They will think they got away with it.
I would be dishonoring my pain.
Forgiveness means excusing what they did.
They have to answer for it first.

beliefs.belief: Forgiving means I have to trust them again.
beliefs.origins: Many believers were taught that real forgiveness means returning to how things were. In families, churches, and marriages, people are sometimes pressured to resume relationships with those who have not changed.
client_words: If I forgive, I have to let them back in.
Forgiving means going back to normal.
I cannot forgive because I cannot trust.
If I keep my distance, I have not truly forgiven.
I have to give another chance.
I owe them access to me.

beliefs.belief: I can't forgive until I feel like forgiving.
beliefs.origins: We assume forgiveness is an emotion, a warm feeling that arrives on its own. When the pain stays, we conclude we have not forgiven and may feel stuck or guilty.
client_words: I do not feel forgiving, so I cannot.
If it were real forgiveness, the pain would be gone.
I am still angry, so I have not forgiven.
I am waiting until my heart is ready.
Forcing it would be fake.
I cannot choose how I feel.

beliefs.belief: They don't deserve to be forgiven.
beliefs.origins: When harm is serious, it is natural to feel that the person has forfeited forgiveness, especially if they have shown no remorse. Our sense of justice is not wrong.
client_words: What they did is unforgivable.
They have not earned it.
They are not sorry.
They should suffer for what they did.
Forgiving would be unfair.
They do not deserve peace.

beliefs.belief: I'm a poor Christian because I can't forgive.
beliefs.origins: When we hear that Christians must forgive, and we cannot, guilt can pile on top of the original hurt. Some of us have tried and failed, been told to “just let it go,” or hear sermons that make forgiveness sound easy.
client_words: A real Christian would have forgiven by now.
Something is wrong with my faith.
God is disappointed in me.
Others forgive more easily.
I am failing God.
I should be over this.

beliefs.belief: If I say no, people will reject me.
beliefs.origins: If love was conditional in our family, or if saying no brought anger, sulking, or punishment, we learned that refusal is dangerous. As adults we say yes to avoid conflict, and then feel resentful, overextended, and unsure whether anyone likes us for who we are.
client_words: If I say no, they will be angry or leave.
I will lose my friends.
Saying no is mean.
I cannot disappoint anyone.
People only like me when I say yes.
Conflict will follow.

beliefs.belief: Setting boundaries is selfish.
beliefs.origins: Many believers were taught to be selfless, to turn the other cheek, and to put others first. Those are good teachings, but they can be bent into the idea that having any limits is sinful.
client_words: Good Christians have no limits.
Saying no is putting myself first.
Selfless people never say no.
I should always be available.
Limits are unloving.
My needs do not count.

beliefs.belief: Conflict always ruins relationships.
beliefs.origins: If conflict in our home meant screaming, silence for days, or violence, we learned to avoid it at all costs. Some churches also teach that disagreement is a lack of unity.
client_words: If we disagree, it is over.
Peace means never arguing.
I must avoid conflict at all costs.
If I bring it up, it will explode.
Good relationships have no conflict.
Silence is safer.

beliefs.belief: I must give people whatever they ask of me.
beliefs.origins: Generous people, caregivers, and helpers can be asked for time, money, rides, listening, and favors without end. If we were raised to think that refusing a request is unloving, we can end up drained and used.
client_words: If someone asks, I have to say yes.
I cannot say no to people in need.
Refusing is unloving.
I must meet every request.
If I do not help, no one will.
I owe everyone my time.

beliefs.belief: A good Christian never gets angry.
beliefs.origins: Many of us learned that anger is always sinful, that nice people never show it, and that Christians should be calm. Where anger was explosive in the home, we may fear it in ourselves.
client_words: Angry feelings mean I am a bad Christian.
I should never feel this way.
Good people stay calm.
If I get angry, I am sinning.
I have to bury my anger.
Anger is always wrong.

beliefs.belief: My spouse should make me happy.
beliefs.origins: Romantic stories may suggest that finding the right spouse ends loneliness and unhappiness. Growing up with little comfort can leave you longing for a partner who will finally meet every need.
client_words: If I feel unhappy, my spouse is failing me.
I should not have to find enjoyment outside our time together.
A good spouse would always make me feel special.
My mood depends entirely on what my spouse does.
If marriage takes work, something must be wrong.
My needs matter, so my spouse should meet all of them.

beliefs.belief: My marriage will never get better.
beliefs.origins: Repeated arguments, broken promises, betrayal, or years of feeling alone can make hopelessness understandable. You may have tried hard without seeing lasting change.
client_words: Nothing we try will matter.
We had another argument, so we have made no progress.
The past proves the future is hopeless.
If change were possible, it would have happened already.
I have to fix the marriage by myself.
Seeking help would only confirm that we have failed.

beliefs.belief: If my spouse loved me, they would know what I need.
beliefs.origins: Early experiences of being overlooked can make having to ask feel painful or humiliating. Romantic messages may teach that true love should understand without words.
client_words: I should not have to ask.
If I tell them, it will not count.
They know exactly what I need and are choosing to ignore it.
A loving spouse would notice every hint.
Asking makes me needy.
If they guess wrong, they do not care.

beliefs.belief: I married the wrong person.
beliefs.origins: Painful differences, unmet expectations, betrayal, or comparison with other couples may lead you to question your choice. Believing that there is one flawless match can turn ordinary disagreements into evidence of a permanent mistake.
client_words: The right person would never disappoint me.
Our differences prove that we should never have married.
Another spouse would solve all these problems.
I made one choice that ruined my whole life.
I must either deny the problems or leave immediately.
Because I regret something, everything about our marriage is wrong.

beliefs.belief: I can't be loved or happy without my spouse.
beliefs.origins: A close marriage can become central to your sense of belonging. Fear of abandonment, bereavement, separation, betrayal, or past rejection may make life without your spouse seem unbearable.
client_words: Without my spouse, nobody could love me.
If I am alone, my life has no meaning.
I could never enjoy anything again.
I must accept anything to keep this relationship.
Needing support means I cannot cope.
Being separated or widowed makes me incomplete as a person.

beliefs.belief: There will never be enough.
beliefs.origins: Growing up with real shortage, hearing worry about bills at the table, going without, or living through a layoff or a lean season can teach the body to expect “not enough.” Even after things improve, the alarm can keep ringing. Constant messages to buy more, have more, and keep up can also make any amount feel small.
client_words: No matter what I earn, it will not be enough.
There is always another bill around the corner.
If I relax, I will run out.
Other people have enough; I never do.
I cannot enjoy anything because I might need the money later.
Good times never last.

beliefs.belief: Anything I have could vanish tomorrow.
beliefs.origins: A sudden loss of a job, a home, a loved one, or savings can teach us that nothing is safe. A parent who lost everything, or who lived in constant fear of loss, may have passed that fear along without a word.
client_words: Whatever I build can be taken away.
I cannot let myself get comfortable.
Just when things are good, something will happen.
I should not get attached to anything.
Having less means losing less.
Safety is an illusion.

beliefs.belief: I must hold on to everything.
beliefs.origins: When money, food, or comfort were scarce, holding on tightly was how a family survived. Saving everything, never wasting, and never letting go can feel like the only safe way.
client_words: If I let go of anything, I will regret it.
I might need it someday.
Throwing things out is wasteful and dangerous.
I cannot give; I need everything I have.
Letting go means losing.
If I hold on tight enough, I will stay safe.

beliefs.belief: Asking for help means I’ve failed.
beliefs.origins: Families that prized independence, or that were ashamed of needing anything, can teach children that asking is weakness. A person who asked for help and was refused, mocked, or made to feel indebted may stop asking altogether.
client_words: A capable person handles it alone.
If I ask, people will think less of me.
I should not need anyone.
Needing help proves I could not cope.
I do not want to owe anyone.
Other people never struggle like this.

beliefs.belief: Life is never stable or safe.
beliefs.origins: Childhood in an unpredictable home, repeated moves, a frightening event, or growing up around constant financial strain can teach the mind that the ground is never solid. When hardship comes often, the nervous system learns to stay on guard, and it can begin to feel as if danger is always near.
client_words: Something bad is always about to happen.
I can never relax.
Nothing in life can be counted on.
I have to stay on guard all the time.
Safety is for other people.
Just when things settle down, they fall apart.
