beliefs.belief: I earned everything; others just didn't try.
beliefs.origins: A family that prized hard work, a career that rewarded effort, or a community that looked down on struggle can teach us that success is simply the result of trying. Because effort really does matter, the belief feels true.
client_words: Anyone who really tried would have what I have.
People who struggle brought it on themselves.
I did this on my own.
I do not owe anyone anything.
If they wanted it, they would have worked harder.
Being generous would only reward laziness.

beliefs.belief: My worth depends on staying wealthy.
beliefs.origins: When a family, a profession, or a social circle measures people by what they own, we can learn that value equals net worth. A parent’s approval may have followed achievement, or a past loss may have made money feel like the only protection against shame.
client_words: If I lost my money, I would be nothing.
I am only as valuable as my portfolio.
People respect me because of what I have.
I cannot stop earning or I will fall apart.
Without wealth I would have no identity.
Rest is for people who have not made it.

beliefs.belief: People only like me for my money.
beliefs.origins: Being asked for loans, gifts, or favors, watching friends change after a promotion or inheritance, or seeing someone use a relationship for gain can make it hard to trust anyone. Family conflict over money can also teach us that affection comes with strings.
client_words: If I had less, no one would be around.
Everyone wants something from me.
I cannot tell who is sincere.
I am safer keeping people at a distance.
Nobody would choose me for me.
Being generous only attracts users.

beliefs.belief: I must never let anyone see me struggle.
beliefs.origins: In families, workplaces, and communities where success is a sign of status, struggle can feel like exposure. A parent who always looked fine, a culture of “keeping up appearances,” or a past experience when vulnerability was used against us can teach us to hide.
client_words: If they knew I was struggling, they would lose respect for me.
I have to look like I have it all together.
Needing help means I have failed.
Struggle is for other people.
I cannot afford to be seen as weak.
I will handle it alone.

beliefs.belief: Money can fix any problem.
beliefs.origins: When money has solved real problems, such as a repair, a medical bill, or a hard season, it is easy to conclude that it can solve everything. Families who handle conflict by paying for it, or who show love with gifts, can pass this lesson on.
client_words: If I just had enough money, this would be solved.
I can pay my way out of anything.
Problems are only a matter of resources.
Giving gifts shows people I care.
Money is the answer to every worry.
If it cannot be bought, it does not matter.

beliefs.belief: My debt proves I'm irresponsible.
beliefs.origins: Debt can come from many roads: a job loss, an illness, a divorce, a family emergency, school, rising prices, or simply choices we now regret. But family and culture often attach one meaning to all of them: “You must have been careless.” If a parent was ashamed of owing money, or if people judged us for it, we may…
client_words: Only careless people end up in debt.
I should have known better.
Everyone can see I cannot manage money.
My debt shows what kind of person I am.
If I were responsible, I would not owe.
I have failed my family.

beliefs.belief: I must hide my money problems.
beliefs.origins: Many of us learned that money is private and that trouble should be kept inside the family. Fear of judgment, embarrassment about status, or a parent who always “kept up appearances” can teach us to hide.
client_words: If anyone knew, I would be humiliated.
I have to look like I have everything under control.
My spouse cannot handle knowing.
It is better to say nothing.
I will fix this quietly.
People would think less of me.

beliefs.belief: I can never get out of this.
beliefs.origins: When bills pile up, interest grows, or one setback follows another, the situation can feel like quicksand. Long stress narrows thinking, and past efforts that failed may make a new plan seem pointless.
client_words: Nothing I do will ever make a difference.
I will be paying this off forever.
There is no way out.
I have tried everything.
This is just my life now.
It is too late to fix it.

beliefs.belief: I don't deserve anything nice.
beliefs.origins: After debt, many people punish themselves: no vacations, no new clothes, no small pleasures, even when there is room for them. Messages that equated owing money with guilt, a parent who said “we can’t afford joy,” or religious teaching that confused simplicity with suffering can all feed this belief.
client_words: After what I did, I do not get nice things.
I should suffer until the debt is paid.
Enjoying anything would be selfish.
My family should do without because of me.
I have to earn the right to be happy.
Small pleasures are a waste.

beliefs.belief: Talking about money is shameful.
beliefs.origins: In many families, money was never discussed, or it was discussed only in anger. Phrases like “Don’t ask what people earn” or “That is none of your business” can grow into the belief that any talk about money is improper.
client_words: Money is not something decent people talk about.
Asking about money is rude.
If I bring it up, I will look greedy.
My spouse and I should not argue about money, so we do not talk.
I would rather not know.
It is not spiritual to care about money.

beliefs.belief: Love is shown through things.
beliefs.origins: In some homes, gifts were the main way love was spoken. A parent who worked long hours may have shown care by providing, buying, and fixing, and may have found it hard to say the words.
client_words: If they really loved me, they would buy me this.
I show my kids I love them by giving them things.
Without gifts, I do not know how to show care.
When money is tight, I cannot be a good parent or spouse.
Gifts prove love.
No present means no love.

beliefs.belief: People like us never get ahead.
beliefs.origins: This message can be spoken or silent. It may have come from a family that worked hard and still struggled, from a neighborhood with few opportunities, or from a parent trying to protect children from disappointment by lowering expectations.
client_words: Nothing ever changes for people like us.
It is not worth trying.
Wanting more is being ungrateful.
If I get ahead, I am leaving my family behind.
The deck is stacked against us.
We are who we are.

beliefs.belief: People like us don't go to college.
beliefs.origins: In some families, no one has gone to college, or college was something others did. Cost, fear of debt, a lack of information, a parent who feared losing a child to a different world, or a school that did not encourage it can all feed this belief.
client_words: College is for other people.
We cannot afford it, so there is no point looking.
I am not smart enough.
If I go, I will not fit in.
My family would not understand.
It is better not to hope.

beliefs.belief: Money is what causes all our fights.
beliefs.origins: Money can feel like the center of family conflict, especially when it was scarce or when arguments about it were loud. Children who grew up hearing fights over bills may link money and conflict for life.
client_words: If we had more money, we would not fight.
Money is the only thing we argue about.
It is safer not to talk about money.
Every argument comes back to money.
We cannot fix this until we are wealthy.
Money ruins everything.

beliefs.belief: Wealthy people can't be trusted.
beliefs.origins: Many of us learned this from a boss who underpaid us, a landlord who ignored repairs, a family who felt looked down on, or a community that felt used. Stories and media can add to it.
client_words: Rich people got there by cheating.
They look down on people like me.
They will always put money first.
I cannot be friends with someone who has that much.
If I become wealthy, I will become like them.
Wealth corrupts everyone.

beliefs.belief: I am what I do for a living.
beliefs.origins: What do you do?” is often the first question we are asked, and the answer can quietly become who we are. A family that prized a certain career, a profession with long training, or a parent whose identity was their job can teach us to merge the two.
client_words: If I am not my job, I do not know who I am.
My title is my identity.
When people ask what I do, that is who I am.
If my work is ordinary, so am I.
Without my role, I disappear.
I only matter when I am working.

beliefs.belief: Without a job, I'm worthless.
beliefs.origins: Losing work, retiring, being laid off, being unable to work because of illness, or caring for children at home can bring a painful sense of having no value. Many of us were taught that productive people matter and the rest do not.
client_words: I contribute nothing without a paycheck.
I am a drain on everyone.
Everyone else is doing something and I am not.
I have no purpose without a job.
I am wasting my life.
People do not respect someone who is not working.

beliefs.belief: Rest must be earned.
beliefs.origins: Many of us grew up where rest was a reward for finishing everything, and the list never ended. Parents who worked without pause, jobs that praised overwork, or cultures that treat busyness as virtue can teach that rest is for people who have done enough.
client_words: I have not done enough to rest.
If I stop, everything will fall apart.
Rest is for lazy people.
I feel guilty when I sit down.
I will rest when everything is finished.
Others are working while I rest.

beliefs.belief: My value depends on how much I earn.
beliefs.origins: When salary becomes the scoreboard, a raise feels like approval and a pay cut feels like a demotion of the self. This can come from families who compared incomes, workplaces that publicly ranked pay, or a culture that treats earnings as a measure of success.
client_words: The more I earn, the more I matter.
If someone earns more than me, they are worth more.
My salary is my report card.
I have to keep climbing to be worth anything.
Making less means being less.
People respect me for my income.

beliefs.belief: If I lose this job, I lose everything.
beliefs.origins: When a household depends on one income, or when a job has also given us our identity, friends, and purpose, the thought of losing it can feel like the end. Past layoffs, an unstable family history, or a workplace that keeps people anxious can add to the fear.
client_words: If this job ends, my life is over.
I would lose my home, my friends, and my future.
I cannot take any risk at work.
I must say yes to everything to stay safe.
There is nothing else for me out there.
I would be nothing.

beliefs.belief: I'm a failure because I lost my job.
beliefs.origins: Losing a job can feel personal even when it is not. Layoffs, closures, health problems, and changes in an industry happen to capable people.
client_words: If I were better, I would still have my job.
I let everyone down.
This proves I was never good enough.
I am a failure.
Everyone else holds on to their jobs.
I should have seen it coming.

beliefs.belief: I'll never recover from this.
beliefs.origins: After a major loss, the future can look closed. Savings shrink, applications go unanswered, and each week of waiting makes the fear grow.
client_words: This is the end of my career.
I will never be financially stable again.
Things will never go back to normal.
It is too late for me to start over.
Nothing I try works.
This is how my life will be from now on.

beliefs.belief: Others must think I'm useless.
beliefs.origins: After a setback, we often imagine what other people are saying. A family member’s silence, a former coworker’s awkward pause, or a friend’s “So what are you doing now?” can feel like judgment.
client_words: Everyone thinks I am a failure.
People are talking about me.
They are being polite, but they pity me.
I cannot face anyone I know.
I have lost everyone’s respect.
They are better than me now.

beliefs.belief: I should be further along by now.
beliefs.origins: Comparison is a quiet thief. Classmates’ promotions, social media updates, a parent’s expectations, or an internal timeline we set long ago can make us feel behind.
client_words: Everyone my age is ahead of me.
I have wasted so much time.
I should have achieved more by now.
It is too late to catch up.
I am behind in every area.
I will never reach where others are.

beliefs.belief: One setback means I've ruined my life.
beliefs.origins: A single event, such as a failed business, a layoff, a lost promotion, or a bad financial decision, can feel like proof that everything is ruined. This is especially strong when we have worked hard to avoid mistakes.
client_words: I ruined everything.
There is no coming back from this.
My whole life is wrecked.
I blew my one chance.
Everything I built is gone.
One mistake has defined me.

beliefs.belief: People with money are better than me.
beliefs.origins: Wealth often comes with confidence, polish, and access, and those can look like superiority. If we grew up with less, were treated as lesser, or were taught to defer to the wealthy, we may keep that stance for life.
client_words: They are smarter than I am.
I should defer to people with more.
I am not in their league.
They deserve more respect.
I am less because I have less.
I should not speak up around them.

beliefs.belief: Where I come from makes me less.
beliefs.origins: A neighborhood, a family name, a region, an accent, or a family’s history can be treated as a mark against us. Teasing, being passed over, or feeling like an outsider at school or work can leave a lasting sense of being less.
client_words: People from where I come from do not amount to much.
I should hide where I grew up.
I will never fit in.
My background is a mark against me.
My accent gives me away.
I come from nothing.

beliefs.belief: I don't belong among successful people.
beliefs.origins: Walking into a conference room, a neighborhood, a church gathering, or a social event where everyone seems more polished can bring a sudden sense of being an imposter. People who moved up from humble beginnings often describe it.
client_words: I am an imposter and they will find out.
I do not belong in this room.
They are on a different level than I am.
I will say something wrong.
I should stay where I am comfortable.
I got here by luck.

beliefs.belief: My clothes, car, or home show my worth.
beliefs.origins: Appearances can feel like a language everyone reads. A parent who dressed up for the neighbors, a school where brands mattered, or a workplace where the car in the parking lot sent a message can teach us to treat possessions as proof of value.
client_words: People judge me by what I drive.
If my house looks small, so am I.
I have to dress the part to be taken seriously.
Nice things prove I have made it.
Having less shows I am less.
I would be embarrassed if people saw my home.

beliefs.belief: Being poor means being lazy or bad.
beliefs.origins: This belief is common because it is comforting: if poverty is always someone’s fault, then we are safe from it. It appears in family sayings, political rhetoric, and even misread proverbs.
client_words: If I were not lazy, I would not be poor.
Poor people just need to try harder.
I am to blame for my situation.
Being poor is my fault.
People think poor people are bad.
I should be ashamed of needing help.

beliefs.belief: Retirement means I'm no longer useful.
beliefs.origins: For many people, work gave structure, status, and purpose. When it ends, whether by choice, health, or company decision, the days can feel empty and the world can seem to stop needing us.
client_words: Nobody needs me anymore.
I have nothing left to give.
My best years are behind me.
I am just waiting around.
I have no purpose without work.
The world has moved on.

beliefs.belief: Caring for others means my needs don't count.
beliefs.origins: Parents, caregivers for aging relatives, and people in helping professions often learn to put themselves last. Family messages like “Don’t be selfish” or religious teaching that confuses sacrifice with self-erasure can add to it.
client_words: My needs are not important.
Taking time for myself is selfish.
Everyone else comes first.
If I stop, everything will fall apart.
I should not need anything.
Good people do not have needs.

beliefs.belief: As a parent, I must provide everything.
beliefs.origins: Parents want the best for their children, and many feel a heavy weight to provide every opportunity. A parent who grew up with little may vow that their children will never lack, and one who grew up with much may fear lowering the standard.
client_words: If my kids lack anything, I have failed.
I have to give them everything I did not have.
Good parents provide every opportunity.
Other parents give their children more.
I must never say no.
It all depends on me.

beliefs.belief: I'm a burden now that I can't work.
beliefs.origins: Illness, injury, disability, or age can limit work, and with it independence and income. Receiving care, relying on family, or needing help with money can feel like a burden to others.
client_words: My family would be better off without me.
I am just a drain on everyone.
I used to contribute and now I cannot.
I am a weight on those I love.
I should not need so much.
I am useless now.

beliefs.belief: Needing help means losing my dignity.
beliefs.origins: Many of us learned that independence is a mark of maturity and that asking for help is a loss of standing. Pride, family pride, or past experiences when help came with humiliation can feed this belief.
client_words: Real adults do not need help.
If I ask, I am admitting defeat.
People will lose respect for me.
I would rather struggle alone than owe anyone.
Taking help means I am weak.
Needing anything is humiliating.

beliefs.belief: If God loved me, I wouldn't be struggling.
beliefs.origins: When money runs short, it is natural to wonder where God is. Many of us were taught, openly or quietly, that love and ease go together: good children are cared for, and loved people are comfortable.
client_words: God must be angry with me.
Other people are not struggling like this, so God must love them more.
If God cared, He would fix this.
Maybe God does not love me the way He loves others.
I must have done something to lose His love.
My hardship proves I am not loved.

beliefs.belief: God has forgotten my needs.
beliefs.origins: When prayers about rent, bills, or work seem to go unanswered, silence can feel like neglect. People who were overlooked as children, whose needs were forgotten by caregivers, often carry the same expectation toward God.
client_words: God has overlooked me.
He answers everyone else’s prayers but mine.
My needs are too small or too ordinary for Him.
I have been waiting too long.
He has moved on from my situation.
No one is looking out for me, not even God.

beliefs.belief: My money problems are God's punishment.
beliefs.origins: When something goes wrong after a mistake, such as a bad purchase, a debt, or a time we cut corners, it is easy to connect the dots and decide God is paying us back. Some families and churches taught that bad things happen to bad people.
client_words: God is making me pay for my mistakes.
I deserve this.
This is what I get for what I did.
God is teaching me a lesson by taking things away.
If I had been better, this would not have happened.
I am being punished.

beliefs.belief: It's all up to me; I can't count on God to provide.
beliefs.origins: People who grew up with unreliable adults often learn to rely only on themselves. A parent who lost jobs, a family that ran out of money, or a time when no one came to help can train a person to carry every burden alone.
client_words: If I do not handle it, no one will.
I cannot rely on anyone, including God.
God helps those who help themselves.
Trusting God is irresponsible.
I have to make it happen.
Rest is a luxury I cannot afford.

beliefs.belief: Worrying about money shows I'm being responsible.
beliefs.origins: Worry can feel like a form of caring. If we stop worrying, we fear we will stop paying attention.
client_words: If I stop worrying, I will get careless.
Worrying keeps me prepared.
Good providers lose sleep over money.
Relaxing about money is irresponsible.
I have to think about it constantly.
Worry shows I care.

beliefs.belief: Wealth proves God is pleased with me.
beliefs.origins: When things go well, it is natural to give thanks. The danger is concluding that success is God’s stamp of approval.
client_words: God is blessing me because I am doing right.
My success shows I am in His favor.
People who struggle must be doing something wrong.
I deserve what I have.
If I lose this, God must be displeased.
My wealth is my reward.

beliefs.belief: If I had enough faith, I wouldn't be poor.
beliefs.origins: Messages that promise wealth to the faithful are common in some preaching, books, and broadcasts. When someone who prays and gives still struggles, the teaching leaves only one conclusion: my faith must be lacking.
client_words: My faith must be weak.
If I believed more, God would provide.
I am not praying hard enough.
I must be doing something wrong.
Other believers have more because they have more faith.
My poverty is my fault spiritually.

beliefs.belief: Being poor means God has rejected me.
beliefs.origins: In many cultures, poverty carries stigma, and that stigma can seep into our view of God. If we have been rejected by people, treated as less, or overlooked at church because of money, it is a short step to feeling that God has turned away from us too.
client_words: God has turned His back on me.
I am not important to God.
He prefers people who have more.
I am on the outside of His blessing.
I am a disappointment to Him.
Even God has given up on me.

beliefs.belief: God only blesses people who succeed.
beliefs.origins: Cultures that celebrate achievement can seep into our picture of God. Churches may spotlight winners and testimonies of success, while those who struggle go unnoticed.
client_words: I have to succeed for God to bless me.
Failure puts me outside His favor.
God favors the capable.
I must hide my struggles.
I have not earned His blessing.
Only winners get blessed.

beliefs.belief: Struggling financially means I'm out of God's will.
beliefs.origins: Many believers equate being in God’s will with everything falling into place. When a job ends or money gets tight, they wonder if they missed a turn.
client_words: I must have missed God’s direction.
This is what happens when I step out of His will.
If I were in His will, things would be smoother.
I made a wrong turn and ruined everything.
God is not guiding me anymore.
I cannot trust my own decisions.

beliefs.belief: My work only matters to God if it's ministry.
beliefs.origins: Many believers hear more about missionaries and pastors than about plumbers, nurses, and clerks. Over time, a divide forms in the mind: spiritual work counts, ordinary work is just a paycheck.
client_words: My job is just a paycheck.
Only church work really counts.
God does not care about my daily tasks.
I am wasting my life in an ordinary job.
Real servants of God are in ministry.
My work is not spiritual.

beliefs.belief: God can't use me without a good job.
beliefs.origins: Job titles, income, and influence can seem like the qualifications for being used by God. When a layoff, health problem, or limited education leaves us without a “good job,” we may believe our usefulness has expired.
client_words: I have nothing to offer without a good job.
God uses people with status.
I am too ordinary to be useful.
I need a better résumé first.
Others are better suited for His work.
My unemployment makes me useless to Him.

beliefs.belief: Rest is laziness, even when God commands it.
beliefs.origins: Families that prized hard work may have called rest “wasting time.” Cultures that celebrate busyness reinforce it. Even people who know the Sabbath is a command may feel guilty for taking it, especially when money is tight and there seems to be more to do than hours to do it.
client_words: I cannot afford to rest.
Resting is lazy.
There is always more to do.
If I rest, I will fall behind.
Others work harder than I do.
I have to earn my rest.

beliefs.belief: If I'm not productive, I'm wasting the life God gave me.
beliefs.origins: Productivity can become a moral standard. Lists, goals, and income can turn into a daily scoreboard.
client_words: Every unproductive minute is a waste.
I must always accomplish something.
Time off is a failure.
Being sick means I am useless.
I am only valuable when I produce.
I will regret all the time I wasted.

beliefs.belief: God values me for what I accomplish.
beliefs.origins: Children who are praised mostly for grades, achievements, or helpfulness often conclude that love is earned. In adulthood this becomes a quiet belief: God is pleased when I produce and disappointed when I do not.
client_words: God is pleased only when I achieve.
I have to earn His approval.
When I fail, He is disappointed.
My worth goes up and down with my results.
I must keep proving myself.
I am loved for what I do.

beliefs.belief: We don't talk about our problems outside the family.
beliefs.origins: Many families, cultures, and churches prize privacy. Some of that is wise: not every struggle belongs on social media.
client_words: What happens at home stays at home.
Talking about it would shame us.
Strong families handle things privately.
No one outside could understand.
If I tell, I am betraying them.
We just do not speak about that.

beliefs.belief: Asking for help is a sign of weakness.
beliefs.origins: Families and cultures that prize self-reliance, whether through farm life, immigrant struggle, military service, or hard times, often teach that needing help is shameful. Children who watched parents never ask learn to white-knuckle through illness, money problems, and sorrow alone.
client_words: Real adults handle things alone.
If I ask, I look weak.
We never needed anyone.
I do not want to be a burden.
Asking means I have failed.
I should be able to manage.

beliefs.belief: I must never bring shame on my family.
beliefs.origins: In many cultures, family honor is central. A child’s failure, divorce, pregnancy, addiction, or leaving the family’s faith or traditions can be treated as a stain on everyone.
client_words: If I fail, my whole family is disgraced.
I cannot let them down.
People will talk about us.
I have to keep up appearances.
My mistake is everyone’s mistake.
I carry the family name.

beliefs.belief: Our family has always been this way, and it can't change.
beliefs.origins: Patterns such as anger, addiction, divorce, poverty, silence, or distance can run for generations, and people often say, “That is just how we are.” Hearing it repeated can make change feel disloyal or impossible.
client_words: This is how we are.
It runs in the family.
We have never done it differently.
Trying to change is pointless.
I will end up like them.
Change would betray the family.

beliefs.belief: I have to live up to what my family expects of me.
beliefs.origins: Families often have unspoken scripts about career, marriage, faith, location, and success. A child may be told, openly or not, what they will be: a doctor, a farmer, a pastor, a parent.
client_words: I owe them the life they planned for me.
If I choose differently, I am betraying them.
I cannot disappoint my parents.
Their approval is worth more than my own path.
I must meet their expectations.
My dreams do not matter.

beliefs.belief: People like me will never be treated fairly.
beliefs.origins: For many, unfair treatment is not a theory: it is experience, from jokes, suspicion, being passed over, or worse. Family stories of injustice add weight.
client_words: The system is rigged against people like me.
No matter what I do, I will be judged first by my background.
Fairness is not for us.
There is no point in trying.
They will never see us as equal.
Things will never change.

beliefs.belief: People like me don't succeed.
beliefs.origins: If we see few examples of people from our background in leadership, college, or business, we may conclude that success is for others. Counselors, teachers, or relatives may have lowered expectations, and the statistics we hear can feel like a sentence.
client_words: Nobody from my background makes it.
I will hit a ceiling.
I do not look like the people who succeed.
Trying is a waste.
They will not give me a chance.
I should not expect much.

beliefs.belief: Because of my background, I'll always be an outsider.
beliefs.origins: Accent, skin color, immigration history, religion, or a different way of speaking or eating can set us apart. Repeated questions like “Where are you really from?” or being left out of social circles reinforce a sense of not belonging.
client_words: I will never fully belong here.
They will always see me as different.
I am too foreign.
There is nowhere I fit.
I have to hide where I am from.
Others have a place and I do not.

beliefs.belief: Everyone from that group is the same.
beliefs.origins: Stereotypes are learned early: from family jokes, news coverage, a bad experience, or a neighborhood’s attitudes. Our minds sort people into categories to save effort, and fear or hurt can harden those categories.
client_words: They are all alike.
You can’t trust any of them.
I know what those people are like.
One bad experience tells me everything.
They are all the same.
I do not need to know them.

beliefs.belief: I'm less valuable because of where I come from.
beliefs.origins: Mockery of an accent, a neighborhood, or a country, or being treated as a representative of a stereotype, teaches us that our origin is a defect. Over time, we may apologize for it, hide it, or conclude it makes us less.
client_words: Where I come from is a disadvantage.
I should be ashamed of my background.
My accent marks me as lesser.
People from my place are worth less.
I have to hide my origin.
I started behind and will stay behind.

beliefs.belief: What other people think of me is what matters most.
beliefs.origins: In close communities, reputation can feel like survival. Gossip, church talk, and neighborhood watchfulness teach us to monitor how we look to others.
client_words: If people think badly of me, I am ruined.
I have to manage how I come across.
Their opinion decides my worth.
I cannot stand being talked about.
I must keep up appearances.
I have to please everyone.

beliefs.belief: I'll never escape where I grew up.
beliefs.origins: Some neighborhoods carry poverty, crime, addiction, or limited opportunity, and people who grow up there may feel marked for life. Others live in small towns where everyone knows their family history.
client_words: I will always be trapped here.
No one gets out.
My past will follow me forever.
I cannot become anything else.
The pull of home is too strong.
I do not know how to live differently.

beliefs.belief: I can't be trusted or respected because of my reputation.
beliefs.origins: A past mistake, a family name, rumors, or a label given in youth can follow us in a community. When people have decided who we are, it can seem pointless to try.
client_words: Everyone already has their opinion of me.
Nothing I do will change it.
I will always be that person.
They will never trust me.
Why try to be better?
My reputation is permanent.

beliefs.belief: If I don't fit in with my community, I'm worthless.
beliefs.origins: Tight-knit communities can offer deep belonging, and they can also demand conformity in politics, faith, lifestyle, or ambition. Those who differ may be quietly shunned.
client_words: If they reject me, I am nothing.
I have to conform to be worth anything.
I do not measure up to what this community wants.
Being different means being less.
I have no value outside them.
Without their approval I am nobody.

beliefs.belief: People in my town will always see me as I was.
beliefs.origins: In small towns and tight communities, people remember. A teenage mistake, a divorce, an addiction, or a family scandal may be recalled for decades.
client_words: They will never forget what I did.
I will always be that person to them.
No matter how I change, they will not see it.
I cannot outlive my past here.
Every look reminds me.
People never change their minds about me.

beliefs.belief: I don't belong anywhere.
beliefs.origins: Moves, divorce, immigration, a church split, a difference in temperament or beliefs, or years of being the odd one out can leave a person feeling that no group is truly theirs. We may feel like visitors in our own lives.
client_words: There is no place for me.
I always feel like a guest.
Every group already has its own.
I do not fit anywhere.
I will always be on the outside.
No one would notice if I left.

beliefs.belief: I have to hide who I really am to be accepted.
beliefs.origins: Many learn early that certain parts of themselves, such as their faith, accent, interests, past, or feelings, bring teasing or rejection. They adapt, mask, and perform.
client_words: If they knew the real me, they would reject me.
I have to act the part.
My true self is too much, or not enough.
I have to edit myself.
I am only accepted because I pretend.
I cannot relax around anyone.

beliefs.belief: If I leave my culture behind, I'm betraying my people.
beliefs.origins: Those who move for education, work, marriage, or faith can feel torn. Family may say, “You think you’re better than us,” or hint that adopting new ways is disloyal.
client_words: If I change, I am abandoning them.
They will think I am better than them.
I owe them my loyalty in everything.
Growing up means leaving them behind.
I am a traitor if I adopt other ways.
I cannot belong to two worlds.

beliefs.belief: Nobody will ever understand where I come from.
beliefs.origins: Hardship, immigration, unusual family situations, poverty, abuse, or an unusual culture can make our story feel unshareable. After awkward or dismissive responses, we stop trying to explain.
client_words: No one has lived what I have.
If I explain, they will not get it.
I will always feel misunderstood.
My story is too different.
It is not worth trying to share.
People like me are not understood.

beliefs.belief: I have to earn my place in any group.
beliefs.origins: Where acceptance was handed out for performance, such as grades, athletics, usefulness, or obedience, we learn that belonging is a wage. In new groups, we over-work, over-give, and fear being found out as ordinary.
client_words: I have to prove myself first.
I have to be useful to be kept.
They will accept me only if I perform.
I cannot just show up.
If I stop earning it, I will be out.
I owe the group before I get a place.

beliefs.belief: Everyone else's life is better than mine.
beliefs.origins: Social media shows other people’s best moments: vacations, new homes, engagements, promotions, happy kids. We compare those highlights to our own full, ordinary days.
client_words: Everyone else is happier than I am.
I am falling behind.
My life is boring and small.
They have it all together.
I am missing out.
What is wrong with my life?

beliefs.belief: If I'm not liked online, I don't matter.
beliefs.origins: Likes, followers, shares, and comments feel like measures of worth, and they trigger the brain’s reward systems. Young people especially can tie self-esteem to numbers.
client_words: No likes means no one cares.
My worth is my follower count.
If it flops, I flopped.
I have to post to be seen.
People who matter get attention.
I am invisible without engagement.

beliefs.belief: I must have the latest things to be happy.
beliefs.origins: Advertising, influencers, and peers keep telling us that the next phone, car, outfit, or gadget will fill the gap. The excitement of a new purchase is real and short-lived, and then the desire resets.
client_words: I will be happy once I get that.
My old one is embarrassing.
Everyone else has the new version.
I deserve the upgrade.
Without it I am falling behind.
The next purchase will satisfy me.

beliefs.belief: What the media says is normal must be right.
beliefs.origins: Television, streaming, music, news, and social media shape what feels ordinary: how people speak, treat each other, spend, relate, and think. Because we see it so often, it can seem like everyone does it and so it must be fine.
client_words: Everyone does it, so it is fine.
If it is on TV, it is normal.
I do not need to question what I watch.
That is just how people live now.
Questioning it makes me old-fashioned.
If it is everywhere, it must be acceptable.

beliefs.belief: If it feels good, it must be okay.
beliefs.origins: Culture often says, “Follow your heart,” and “If it feels right, do it.” Feelings are real and important, but they are not reliable moral guides, especially when tired, hurt, tempted, or in a rush. This belief can lead to choices we later regret.
client_words: If it feels right, it is right.
My feelings tell me what is true.
I deserve to feel good.
If no one is hurt, it is fine.
I will not know until I try it.
My heart cannot lead me wrong.

beliefs.belief: I have to look a certain way to be loved.
beliefs.origins: Comments about weight, clothes, skin, and hair, a parent’s own struggles with appearance, school teasing, and a constant stream of edited images teach that love goes to the attractive. Dating and social pressures reinforce it.
client_words: No one will love me unless I look right.
I have to lose weight to be loved.
I am not attractive enough to be valued.
Beautiful people are loved more.
I must hide my flaws.
If I let myself go, I will be alone.

beliefs.belief: I'm ugly, and nothing can change that.
beliefs.origins: Words spoken in childhood, teasing, comparisons, or photographs can fasten the label “ugly” to a person for life. Mirrors then confirm what we expect to see, and we may avoid photos, intimacy, or mirrors altogether.
client_words: I am hideous.
I always look wrong.
No one could find me attractive.
I cannot stand to see myself.
Nothing will help.
Everyone sees my flaws first.

beliefs.belief: My body determines my worth.
beliefs.origins: Fitness culture, medical anxiety, fashion, and sexual objectification tell us that our value is how our bodies look or perform. Illness, injury, aging, and weight changes can then feel like losses of worth, not merely of function.
client_words: I am only as valuable as my body looks or performs.
If my body fails, I fail.
My body is the problem.
Aging means losing value.
I am worth more when I am thin or fit.
I hate my body.

beliefs.belief: I'm too old, too heavy, or too plain to matter.
beliefs.origins: Culture often treats youth, thinness, and polish as the standard and quietly sidelines everyone else. Over time, we may feel invisible in stores, workplaces, dating, even church.
client_words: No one notices me anymore.
I am past my usefulness.
I do not have the right look.
People like me do not count.
I should hide.
I have nothing to offer.

beliefs.belief: I'll be happy once I look the way I'm supposed to.
beliefs.origins: The “when I lose X pounds, get this procedure, or fix this feature” story is persuasive. Each goal postpones happiness, and when it is reached, a new flaw appears.
client_words: Once I look right, my life will start.
I cannot enjoy anything until I change.
Happy people are attractive.
I will date, travel, or be photographed when I look better.
Then I will be at peace with myself.
I am waiting for the real me.

beliefs.belief: My worth depends on my success.
beliefs.origins: Praise for good grades, wins, promotions, and paychecks teaches that we are loved for what we achieve. In competitive cultures, success becomes the scorecard of worth, and failure feels like personal defect.
client_words: I am what I achieve.
If I stop succeeding, I am nothing.
My value goes up and down with results.
I have to keep proving myself.
Failure means I am a failure.
I have to win to matter.

beliefs.belief: If I don't have enough money, I'm a failure.
beliefs.origins: In a culture that equates money with competence, financial struggle can feel like personal failure. Layoffs, illness, caregiving, family obligations, and rising costs create shortfalls that have nothing to do with character, yet shame follows.
client_words: If I had been smarter, I would have more.
Money problems prove I am a failure.
Everyone else is doing better.
I should be further ahead.
I am a disappointment to my family.
I cannot hold my head up.

beliefs.belief: Money and things will make me happy.
beliefs.origins: We are surrounded by messages that the right income and possessions deliver contentment. Seeing the relief money brings in a crisis reinforces it.
client_words: I will be happy when I earn more.
More money would fix everything.
The next raise will do it.
Things make life good.
I need more to feel secure.
If I could just afford that, I would be content.

beliefs.belief: I must keep up with everyone around me.
beliefs.origins: Neighborhood, church, school, workplace, and family can set an unspoken pace: the right house, car, vacation, school, wardrobe. Falling behind feels like being judged.
client_words: Everyone else has more.
If I do not keep up, I will be judged.
I have to match my neighbors.
I cannot let my family fall behind.
Slowing down is losing.
What will people think?

beliefs.belief: Winning is everything, and losing means I'm nothing.
beliefs.origins: Sports, school, business, and even church ministries can teach that only winners matter. Parents who cheer wins and sulk over losses, coaches who shame mistakes, and a culture that celebrates champions make losing feel like disgrace.
client_words: If I lose, I am a loser.
Second place is failure.
I have to win to be valued.
I cannot stand losing.
Winners matter and losers do not.
I would rather not try than lose.

beliefs.belief: Good Christians never struggle.
beliefs.origins: Testimonies that jump from “then” to “now,” cheerful greetings, and unspoken rules about “fine” teach us that struggle is a mark against faith. People hide anxiety, doubt, marriage trouble, and sin, so everyone appears to be doing well alone.
client_words: Everyone else at church has it together.
If I struggle, my faith is weak.
I must say I am fine.
Real Christians do not feel this way.
I would be judged if they knew.
I am the only one.

beliefs.belief: I must look perfect to be accepted at church.
beliefs.origins: Dressing up, saying the right things, and keeping family problems private can turn church into a stage. Newcomers and those with messy lives sense that they do not match and either perform or leave.
client_words: I have to look put together.
They would not want me if they knew.
I have to hide my mess.
Everyone else is polished.
I do not fit in.
I must perform.

beliefs.belief: If I doubt, I'm a bad Christian.
beliefs.origins: Many were taught that questions are sinful and faith means never wondering. Seasons of loss, unanswered prayer, or hard questions then bring fear and shame.
client_words: Real believers never doubt.
My questions prove I do not believe.
God is angry at my doubts.
I cannot tell anyone.
I am losing my faith.
I should not ask.

beliefs.belief: My church's rules are the same as God's love.
beliefs.origins: Where rules about dress, music, entertainment, or conduct are taught as the heart of faith, breaking one can feel like losing God’s favor. We confuse a community’s customs with God’s character and cannot tell where the church ends and God begins.
client_words: If I break a rule, God is angry.
The rules are what God wants.
I am only loved if I conform.
If they disapprove, God does too.
I am safe when I follow every rule.
I cannot question.

beliefs.belief: If I leave my church, I'm leaving God.
beliefs.origins: Some churches teach, openly or quietly, that they are the only true place to meet God. After conflict, hurt, a move, or changing convictions, members stay out of fear.
client_words: This church is my only connection to God.
If I leave, I will lose Him.
Leaving is betrayal.
They will say I fell away.
I cannot find God anywhere else.
I must stay no matter what.

beliefs.belief: Strong people don't show emotion.
beliefs.origins: Families, sports, the military, workplaces, and some churches praise those who “keep it together.” Boys especially hear “Don’t cry.” We learn to bottle feelings, which then leak out as anger, numbness, or physical tension.
client_words: Tears are weakness.
I have to hold it together.
Feelings get in the way.
I should not need anyone.
Showing emotion makes me a burden.
I will fall apart if I let it out.

beliefs.belief: Needing counseling means I have weak faith.
beliefs.origins: Some were taught that prayer and Bible reading should be enough, and that anxiety or sadness shows a lack of trust. Seeking a counselor then feels like admitting spiritual failure.
client_words: If I trusted God more, I would not need help.
Counseling is for people without faith.
I should handle this through prayer alone.
Going means I failed spiritually.
People will think my faith is weak.
God should be enough.

beliefs.belief: If I just prayed more, I wouldn't feel this way.
beliefs.origins: Well-meaning people may say, “Just pray about it,” or “Give it to God,” leaving the suffering person feeling guilty. They pray more, feel no relief, and conclude that something is wrong with them or with their faith.
client_words: If I had more faith, I would feel better.
My prayers must not be good enough.
Something is wrong with my relationship with God.
I should not feel this way.
God is withholding relief.
I need to pray harder.

beliefs.belief: People will think I'm crazy if they know.
beliefs.origins: Stigma about anxiety, depression, trauma, and other struggles teaches us to hide them. Early experiences of being dismissed, mocked, or whispered about confirm the fear.
client_words: They will see me as unstable.
I have to keep it a secret.
No one would understand.
I will be treated differently.
I will lose respect.
I am the only one this happens to.

beliefs.belief: I should be able to handle this on my own.
beliefs.origins: Self-reliance is praised, and asking for help can feel like failure. Some learned early that no one would help, so they learned to cope alone.
client_words: I should be able to manage.
Asking for help is weakness.
I do not want to burden anyone.
I have always handled things alone.
If I need help, I have failed.
No one will help anyway.

beliefs.belief: Real men don't cry or ask for help.
beliefs.origins: Boys hear “Man up” and “Stop crying” from family, coaches, and peers. They learn to hide fear, sadness, and need, and later struggle to ask for help even when they are hurting.
client_words: Men do not show weakness.
I should handle it myself.
Crying is for the weak.
Asking for help means I am less of a man.
I have to be the rock.
I cannot let anyone see me struggle.

beliefs.belief: A good woman puts everyone else first.
beliefs.origins: Girls often learn to be helpful, agreeable, and self-sacrificing. Mothers modeling endless giving, church examples of serving, and praise for “selflessness” can leave women exhausted and resentful, unsure whether they are permitted needs of their own.
client_words: If I take time for me, I am selfish.
Everyone else comes first.
My needs do not count.
A good woman never says no.
I must keep everyone happy.
I am responsible for others’ happiness.

beliefs.belief: I'm not a real man or woman if I don't measure up.
beliefs.origins: Culture, family, and church set lists of what “real” men and women do: earn, protect, cook, parent, look a certain way. Singleness, infertility, job loss, illness, or differing gifts can feel like failing at manhood or womanhood.
client_words: A real man provides.
A real woman has children.
I am failing at being who I should be.
I do not fit the mold.
Others measure up and I do not.
My circumstances prove I am less.

beliefs.belief: I must be the strong one, no matter what.
beliefs.origins: The oldest child, the caregiver, the spouse who “keeps it together,” or the one who learned early that no one else would. Others depend on us, and we feel we have no right to fall apart.
client_words: If I fall apart, everything falls apart.
No one else can handle this.
I do not get to be weak.
Others depend on me.
I have to hold it together.
I cannot let anyone down.

beliefs.belief: My role is fixed, and I can't be more than that.
beliefs.origins: Family, culture, or church may tell us who we are allowed to be: the helper, the provider, the quiet one, the one who never leaves. Dreams are dismissed, abilities overlooked, and we shrink to fit.
client_words: This is all I am allowed to be.
I cannot change what is expected of me.
My dreams do not matter.
It is too late to be anything else.
I was born for this role only.
People would not accept me in another role.

beliefs.belief: The people who disagree with me are evil.
beliefs.origins: Constant exposure to outrage, friends who share one view, and media that profits from anger teach us to see the other side as enemies. Friendships and families fracture.
client_words: They are the problem.
They want to destroy the country.
Anyone who thinks that is a bad person.
There is no good in them.
I cannot be friends with them.
I have to fight them.

beliefs.belief: Things will never get better in this country.
beliefs.origins: Every generation has seen decline, and today’s news cycle makes the problems seem endless. After disappointment with leaders and policies, hopelessness sets in, and we withdraw or grow bitter.
client_words: It is all going downhill.
Nothing we do matters.
The best days are behind us.
No leader can fix this.
It is hopeless.
I want to give up on it.

beliefs.belief: My vote, my voice, and my life don't matter.
beliefs.origins: Feeling unheard by officials, lost in large systems, or outvoted again and again can make participation seem pointless. Some also grew up in settings where speaking up was punished.
client_words: One voice changes nothing.
No one listens to people like me.
Why bother?
The system ignores me.
I am invisible.
My life is small.

beliefs.belief: If the right people were in power, I would finally be safe.
beliefs.origins: Elections are framed as life-or-death, and each side warns of catastrophe if the other wins. Fear and hope get attached to leaders, and our sense of safety rises and falls with the polls.
client_words: If they win, we are doomed.
Only the right leader can protect me.
My safety depends on elections.
I will not be okay until they are in charge.
The other side will ruin everything.
I must win.

beliefs.belief: I can't trust anyone in authority.
beliefs.origins: Abuse of power, broken promises, scandals, or a harsh parent or boss can teach that people in charge are dangerous or corrupt. We become suspicious, defensive, or rebellious, even toward good leaders.
client_words: All leaders are corrupt.
They will use me.
I have to protect myself from them.
Authority means danger.
I trust no one in charge.
They are all the same.

beliefs.belief: The world is getting worse and worse.
beliefs.origins: News thrives on alarm, and a steady feed of tragedy gives the impression that everything is collapsing. Older generations may say, “It was better in my day.” Anxiety rises and joy and hope fade.
client_words: Everything is falling apart.
It is worse than ever.
There is no good news.
The future looks dark.
I cannot stand to watch.
Nothing is safe anymore.

beliefs.belief: I can never be safe.
beliefs.origins: Trauma, accidents, crime, illness, or frightening events can convince the mind that danger is everywhere. The body stays on alert, and the world feels like a minefield.
client_words: Danger is everywhere.
Something bad will happen.
I cannot relax.
Nowhere is safe.
I cannot protect myself or my family.
I have to watch constantly.

beliefs.belief: Terrible things are about to happen to me.
beliefs.origins: After loss, a bad diagnosis, trauma, or a pattern of anxious thinking, the mind keeps scanning for the next blow. Sleep and concentration suffer, and the future feels like a threat.
client_words: Something awful is coming.
I can feel it.
I always get bad news.
I cannot relax.
I am waiting for the other shoe to drop.
I will not be able to handle it.

beliefs.belief: I must stay on guard all the time.
beliefs.origins: Past betrayal, trauma, or a chaotic home taught that relaxing leads to harm. Hypervigilance feels like protection, but it exhausts the body and mind, strains relationships, and keeps us from rest.
client_words: If I relax, something bad happens.
I have to watch everything.
Letting my guard down is dangerous.
Peace is naive.
I am the only protector.
I am always bracing.

beliefs.belief: I can't trust anybody.
beliefs.origins: Betrayal by a parent, spouse, friend, church leader, or institution can convince us that everyone will eventually hurt us. We keep people at arm’s length.
client_words: Everyone lets me down.
If I trust, I will be hurt.
People cannot be relied on.
I am safer alone.
I will never open up again.
They all have an agenda.

beliefs.belief: God is punishing me for my many sins.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that every illness, loss, or hardship is God’s punishment for something you did. Parents or caretakers who punished harshly and kept score of every wrong.
client_words: This trouble is God paying me back for what I’ve done.
I’ve sinned too much to expect anything but punishment.
Every bad thing that happens is because of my sin.
God may forgive, but He still makes me pay.
I deserve this.
If I had lived better, this wouldn’t be happening.

beliefs.belief: If there is a God, he would not let this happen.
beliefs.origins: A painful loss, illness, betrayal, injustice, or abuse that seemed senseless. Prayers for protection or healing that were not answered the way you hoped.
client_words: A loving God would never allow this.
Where was God when this happened?
If God were real, He would have stopped it.
Either God doesn’t care, or He isn’t there.
My prayers didn’t work, so maybe faith is a lie.
I can’t trust a God who lets things like this happen.

beliefs.belief: God is disappointed in me.
beliefs.origins: A parent who was often critical, hard to please, or quietly disappointed. High expectations at home or at church that you never felt you met.
client_words: God must be tired of me by now.
I keep letting God down.
Nothing I do is ever good enough for God.
God expected more from me.
If I were really a Christian, I wouldn’t still struggle with this.
God sighs when He looks at me.

beliefs.belief: God is too distant or too busy to care about me.
beliefs.origins: A parent who was absent, emotionally distant, or too busy to notice you. Growing up feeling that your needs were a bother.
client_words: God has bigger things to worry about than me.
My problems are too small for God to care about.
God is far away.
I pray, but nobody is listening.
God takes care of other people, but not me.
I’m on my own.

beliefs.belief: God loves some people more than others.
beliefs.origins: Growing up with a parent who had a favorite child, or being compared with a brother, sister, or classmate. Watching others receive blessings, healing, or answered prayers you did not.
client_words: God has favorites, and I’m not one of them.
Their blessings prove that God loves them more.
God answers their prayers but not mine.
I’m a second-class Christian.
God uses other people; He just puts up with me.
If God loved me as much, my life would look like theirs.

beliefs.belief: I need a priest, a saint, or Mary to bring my prayers to God.
beliefs.origins: Being taught as a child that ordinary people should not speak to God directly. A church culture where only clergy prayed aloud or led worship.
client_words: God won’t listen if I pray on my own.
My prayers aren’t good enough to reach God.
Someone holier than me has to ask for me.
I don’t know the right words, so I shouldn’t pray.
God is too important to hear from someone like me.
I have to go through the proper channels.

beliefs.belief: Jesus saved me, but now it’s up to me to stay acceptable.
beliefs.origins: Hearing that grace saves you, but then being judged by rules, attendance, and appearance. A parent whose love depended on good behavior.
client_words: One more slip and God will be done with me.
I have to keep proving I’m really saved.
Grace got me in, but now it’s all on me.
I’m only as acceptable as my last good day.
If I stop trying hard, God will pull away.
I have to make up for my failures.

beliefs.belief: Jesus is one good way to God among many.
beliefs.origins: A culture that values tolerance and says every path leads to the same place. Friends or family of other faiths whom you love and respect.
client_words: All religions are basically the same.
It doesn’t matter what you believe as long as you’re sincere.
Saying Jesus is the only way is unloving.
Jesus was a great teacher, nothing more.
Good people will get to God however they choose.
I don’t want to seem narrow-minded.

beliefs.belief: Jesus doesn’t understand what I’m going through.
beliefs.origins: Pictures of Jesus as calm, untouched, and far above ordinary struggles. Being told to “just have faith” when you were hurting.
client_words: Nobody understands what this is like.
Jesus never had to deal with anything like this.
He’s God, so it was easy for Him.
My pain is too unusual for Him to relate to.
He’s disappointed that I’m struggling.
I have to go through this alone.

beliefs.belief: Jesus died for other people’s sins, but not ones as bad as mine.
beliefs.origins: Deep shame about something in your past. Being told by a parent or church that certain sins put you beyond help.
client_words: What I did is too terrible to forgive.
Grace is for other people, not me.
If people knew, they’d agree I’m beyond saving.
I’ve sinned too many times for God to keep forgiving.
God forgives small sins, but mine are different.
I don’t deserve to be forgiven.

beliefs.belief: If I don’t speak in tongues, I don’t have the Holy Spirit.
beliefs.origins: A church where speaking in tongues was treated as the main proof of being a real believer. Feeling left out or judged when others prayed in tongues and you did not.
client_words: I must not really be saved.
Something is wrong with me spiritually.
God gave the Spirit to everyone but me.
I’m a second-class Christian.
If I had more faith, I would speak in tongues.
Others are closer to God than I am.

beliefs.belief: If the Spirit were in me, I would never struggle.
beliefs.origins: Testimonies that made the Christian life sound like instant, total victory. Being told that struggling with sin, sadness, or fear proves a lack of faith.
client_words: Real Christians don’t struggle like this.
If I still fight this, the Spirit must not be in me.
Everyone else has victory but me.
I should be past this by now.
My struggle proves I’m a fake.
God must be giving up on me.

beliefs.belief: I have committed the unpardonable sin.
beliefs.origins: A frightening sermon about blasphemy against the Spirit. A blasphemous or angry thought that popped into your mind and would not go away.
client_words: I’ve gone too far and God can never forgive me.
That thought proves I blasphemed the Spirit.
It’s too late for me.
I keep checking, and I still don’t feel forgiven.
God has turned His back on me forever.
There’s no point in praying anymore.

beliefs.belief: The Spirit’s leading always comes as a strong feeling.
beliefs.origins: Hearing people say “God told me” or “I felt led” about every choice. A church that put more weight on impressions than on Scripture and wise counsel.
client_words: I can’t decide until I feel sure.
If I don’t feel it, God isn’t leading me.
That strong feeling must be from God.
I must have missed God because I felt nothing.
Other people hear from God; I don’t.
My anxiety must be the Spirit warning me.

beliefs.belief: My spiritual gifts don’t matter as much as other people’s.
beliefs.origins: A church culture that celebrated only up-front gifts like preaching, singing, or leading. Being overlooked or compared with a more talented sibling or friend.
client_words: What I do doesn’t really count.
God uses other people, not me.
I don’t have any real gifts.
Nobody would miss what I do.
I’m just a background person.
If I were more gifted, I’d matter more.

beliefs.topic: The Supernatural: The Devil, Demons & Angels
beliefs.belief: Every problem I have is a spiritual attack.
beliefs.origins: A church culture that blamed the devil for flat tires, illness, and bad moods alike. Frightening teaching about demons that left you watchful and anxious.
client_words: The enemy is behind everything that goes wrong.
If I’m tired or sad, I’m under attack.
I have to fight spiritually every time something breaks.
This illness must be demonic.
Nothing bad ever happens by accident.
My choices have nothing to do with my problems.

beliefs.topic: The Supernatural: The Devil, Demons & Angels
beliefs.belief: Satan has power over me, and I am helpless.
beliefs.origins: Frightening stories or movies about demonic power. Teaching that focused more on the devil’s strength than on Christ’s victory.
client_words: The devil is stronger than I am.
I can’t fight this.
Evil has a hold on me I can’t break.
God isn’t protecting me.
I’m just a victim of spiritual forces.
There’s nothing I can do.

beliefs.topic: The Supernatural: The Devil, Demons & Angels
beliefs.belief: I am under a generational curse.
beliefs.origins: Seeing the same problems repeat in your family, such as addiction, divorce, anger, or depression. Teaching that the sins of parents automatically bring a curse on children.
client_words: I’m doomed to repeat my parents’ mistakes.
My family is cursed.
There’s no escaping what runs in my family.
My children are cursed because of me.
I need a special prayer to break this.
God is punishing me for what my ancestors did.

beliefs.topic: The Supernatural: The Devil, Demons & Angels
beliefs.belief: My loved one has become an angel watching over me.
beliefs.origins: Words of comfort at a funeral, such as “Heaven gained another angel.” Sympathy cards, songs, and movies. A deep wish to still feel your loved one near you.
client_words: My loved one is my guardian angel now.
They’re watching everything I do.
If I let go of this, I’ll lose them completely.
They’re still here because they’re an angel.
I can talk to them instead of God.
Heaven needed another angel.

beliefs.topic: The Supernatural: The Devil, Demons & Angels
beliefs.belief: I should pray to angels for help.
beliefs.origins: Popular books, gift items, and media that encourage “calling on your angels.” Feeling that God is too big or distant to bother, while angels seem closer and more approachable. New Age spirituality mixed with Christian language.
client_words: My angels will protect me if I ask them.
God is too busy, so I’ll ask an angel.
Angels are easier to talk to than God.
I need to call on the right angel for this problem.
Praying to angels is just extra help.
God won’t mind if I go to them instead.

beliefs.belief: Strong emotions mean my faith is weak.
beliefs.origins: Being told as a child to stop crying or calm down. A church culture that valued always looking happy and peaceful.
client_words: If I trusted God, I wouldn’t feel this way.
Christians shouldn’t cry this much.
My feelings prove I’m spiritually weak.
I have to hide how I really feel.
God is disappointed when I’m upset.
Strong Christians are always calm.

beliefs.belief: Depression and anxiety are always caused by sin.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that every emotional struggle comes from unconfessed sin or lack of faith. Well-meaning friends who asked, “What are you doing wrong?” when you were hurting.
client_words: If I weren’t sinning, I wouldn’t be depressed.
My anxiety proves I don’t trust God.
I must have done something to deserve this.
God is punishing me with these feelings.
If I confess enough, this will go away.
Christians who are depressed aren’t right with God.

beliefs.belief: Counseling or medication shows a lack of faith.
beliefs.origins: Hearing that Christians should “just pray more” instead of getting help. Distrust of psychology because some counselors dismissed faith.
client_words: If I had more faith, I wouldn’t need help.
Taking medicine means I don’t trust God.
Counseling is for people who aren’t right with God.
I should be able to pray this away.
People at church will think less of me.
Getting help means I’ve failed spiritually.

beliefs.belief: My body and its desires are shameful.
beliefs.origins: Being shamed as a child about your body, appearance, or normal curiosity. Teaching that treated the body as evil and only the soul as good.
client_words: My body is something to be ashamed of.
Having desires makes me sinful.
God only cares about my soul.
I hate the way I was made.
Pleasure is always wrong.
I need to punish or ignore my body.

beliefs.belief: Feeling angry is always a sin.
beliefs.origins: A home where anger was frightening, violent, or forbidden. Being punished for showing any frustration as a child.
client_words: Good Christians never get angry.
I’m sinning just by feeling this.
I have to stuff my anger down.
If I’m angry, God is angry with me.
Anger always hurts people.
I can’t admit I’m upset.

beliefs.belief: I have sinned too much to be forgiven.
beliefs.origins: Years of the same struggle, with many failed promises to change. A long list of regrets that seems to grow every day.
client_words: I’ve used up all my chances.
God must be tired of forgiving me.
I keep failing, so there’s no hope.
There’s a limit, and I’ve reached it.
I’ve sinned too many times to come back.
God forgives others, but my list is too long.

beliefs.belief: If I feel guilty, I must be guilty.
beliefs.origins: A sensitive or anxious conscience that sounds the alarm over small things. Growing up being blamed for others’ problems or moods.
client_words: I feel bad, so I must have done something wrong.
Even after I confess, I still feel guilty, so I’m not forgiven.
I’m responsible for how everyone feels.
If I relax, I must be ignoring some sin.
My conscience is always right.
Guilt is how I know I’m a good person.

beliefs.belief: A good Christian always feels guilty.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that stressed sin and unworthiness far more than grace and joy. Feeling that relaxing or being happy is spiritually careless.
client_words: If I don’t feel guilty, I must be proud.
Feeling bad keeps me humble.
Joy is for people who don’t take sin seriously.
I don’t deserve to feel at peace.
God expects me to keep feeling sorry.
A good Christian is always aware of how bad he is.

beliefs.belief: Being tempted is the same as sinning.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that every unwanted thought or desire is a sin. A sensitive conscience that treats passing thoughts as moral failures.
client_words: Having that thought means I’ve already sinned.
A good Christian would never be tempted like this.
I’m disgusting for even thinking that.
Since I’ve already sinned in my mind, I might as well act on it.
Temptation proves I’m not saved.
God is angry every time I’m tempted.

beliefs.belief: Some sins can’t be forgiven until I confess them to a priest.
beliefs.origins: Church teaching that tied forgiveness of serious sins to confession with a priest. Fear of dying before you could get to confession.
client_words: God won’t forgive me until I go to confession.
This sin is too serious for just praying.
If I die before confession, I’m lost.
I’m too ashamed to confess, so I’m stuck.
My prayers alone don’t count.
Someone else has to declare me forgiven.

beliefs.belief: Whatever my church teaches must be biblical.
beliefs.origins: Growing up in a church that discouraged questions. Deep loyalty to a pastor or denomination that helped you.
client_words: If my church says it, it must be true.
Checking the Bible for myself would be disloyal.
My pastor is never wrong.
Asking questions shows a lack of faith.
Other churches are wrong, so mine must be right about everything.
I don’t need to read the Bible; my church tells me what it says.

beliefs.belief: Truth is whatever feels right to me.
beliefs.origins: A culture that says “follow your heart” and “live your truth.” Hurt from rigid rules that made you distrust any outside authority. Wanting to avoid conflict by letting everyone decide for themselves.
client_words: If it feels right, it must be right.
My truth is just as valid as anyone else’s.
No one can tell me what’s true for me.
If I feel peace about it, God must approve.
Rules are just other people’s opinions.
I’ll know the truth by how it feels.

beliefs.belief: If a teaching makes me feel good, it must be from God.
beliefs.origins: Popular preaching that focuses mainly on comfort, success, and self-improvement. Past hurt from harsh teaching, which makes any challenge feel unsafe.
client_words: That sermon felt great, so it must be true.
God would never say anything that makes me uncomfortable.
If a teaching challenges me, it must be wrong.
Real Christianity always makes you feel good.
I only listen to teachers who encourage me.
Correction is from the enemy.

beliefs.belief: If a leader quotes Scripture, what he says must be true.
beliefs.origins: Respect for spiritual leaders, taught from childhood. Leaders who used Bible verses to demand obedience or silence questions.
client_words: He quoted the Bible, so I have to obey.
I can’t question a leader who knows Scripture.
If I disagree, I’m disagreeing with God.
He knows the Bible better than I do, so he must be right.
Using verses proves he’s from God.
I’m not smart enough to check.

beliefs.belief: Church tradition carries the same authority as Scripture.
beliefs.origins: Growing up where long-standing customs were treated as unquestionable. Hearing “we’ve always done it this way” as if it were God’s command.
client_words: If my church has always done it, God must require it.
Questioning tradition is questioning God.
Our customs are just as holy as the Bible.
I’ll be in trouble with God if I don’t follow every tradition.
Tradition is the same as truth.
Changing anything is a betrayal.

beliefs.belief: God forgives, but He never forgets.
beliefs.origins: People in your life who said they forgave you but kept bringing up the past. A parent who held old mistakes over your head.
client_words: God is keeping a record of everything I’ve done.
Someday He’ll bring it all up again.
I may be forgiven, but God still sees me as that person.
My past will always count against me.
God remembers, so I can never really be clean.
He forgave me, but He’s still disappointed.

beliefs.belief: I must pay for my sins through suffering.
beliefs.origins: Being punished harshly as a child and learning that pain makes things right. Feeling that forgiveness is too easy unless you hurt for it.
client_words: I don’t deserve to be happy after what I did.
I have to suffer to make it right.
If I’m hurting, at least I’m paying.
God’s forgiveness is too easy; I need to earn it.
I’ll punish myself so God doesn’t have to.
Good things shouldn’t happen to me.

beliefs.belief: Forgiving means I must trust them again.
beliefs.origins: Being told to “forgive and forget” after being hurt or abused. Pressure to restore a relationship quickly so things look peaceful.
client_words: If I really forgave, I’d let them back in.
Setting limits means I haven’t forgiven.
A good Christian trusts everyone again.
I have to act like nothing happened.
If I keep my distance, I’m holding a grudge.
Forgiving means letting them hurt me again.

beliefs.belief: God has forgiven me, but I can never forgive myself.
beliefs.origins: A mistake that caused real harm to someone you love. High personal standards that make failure feel unbearable.
client_words: I’ll never forgive myself for what I did.
God may have forgiven me, but I can’t.
If I let it go, it means I don’t care.
I have to keep feeling bad to show I’m sorry.
I don’t deserve peace.
I am the worst person I know.

beliefs.belief: Forgiving means pretending it didn’t hurt.
beliefs.origins: Being told to “just get over it” when you were hurt. Family rules that said not to talk about painful things.
client_words: If I’ve forgiven, I shouldn’t still hurt.
Talking about the pain means I’m bitter.
I have to act like it was no big deal.
Christians should get over things quickly.
Admitting it hurt would make me unforgiving.
If I still feel sad, I haven’t really forgiven.

beliefs.belief: I am saved by my good works.
beliefs.origins: Believing that good people go to heaven and bad people do not. Being taught that church attendance, giving, or service earns God’s favor.
client_words: I’m a good person, so God will accept me.
If my good deeds outweigh my bad ones, I’ll be fine.
I have to keep doing more to be saved.
God owes me for all I’ve done.
I’m better than most people, so I’m safe.
If I stop serving, I’ll lose my salvation.

beliefs.belief: I can never really know whether I am saved.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that stressed fear and uncertainty about salvation. Worry that you did not pray the right prayer or did not mean it enough.
client_words: I can never be sure I’m saved.
Maybe I didn’t mean it enough.
If I really were saved, I wouldn’t doubt.
I have to keep checking whether I’m saved.
Only super-spiritual people can be sure.
It would be prideful to say I know I’m saved.

beliefs.belief: One more sin and God will give up on me.
beliefs.origins: A parent or authority who gave “last chances” and then gave up. Threats that you would lose God’s love if you kept failing.
client_words: This is my last chance.
If I mess up again, God is done with me.
God’s patience must be almost gone.
I have to be perfect from now on, or I’m lost.
God gives up on people like me.
One more failure and it’s over.

beliefs.belief: I must suffer in purgatory before I can be with God.
beliefs.origins: Teaching about purgatory from childhood. Fear of suffering after death for sins you have not fully made up for.
client_words: I’ll have to suffer a long time before I see God.
My sins aren’t fully paid for yet.
I’m terrified of what happens after I die.
I have to suffer more now to shorten it later.
My loved one is suffering because of me.
Christ’s death covered some of my sins, but not all.

beliefs.belief: Being raised in a Christian family makes me a Christian.
beliefs.origins: Growing up in church and always identifying as a Christian. Being baptized or confirmed as a child without understanding it.
client_words: I was born a Christian.
My parents’ faith covers me.
I’ve always gone to church, so I’m fine.
I was baptized as a baby, so I don’t need anything else.
My family name speaks for me.
I don’t need a personal relationship with Jesus.

beliefs.belief: If I had enough faith, God would have healed me.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that God always heals when faith is strong enough. Being told your illness continues because you doubt.
client_words: My illness is my fault for not believing enough.
God would heal me if my faith were stronger.
Other people have more faith than I do.
I must be doing something wrong spiritually.
If I admit I’m sick, I’m confessing doubt.
God is disappointed in my weak faith.

beliefs.belief: If I give more, God must give me more.
beliefs.origins: Preaching that promises financial return for giving (“sow a seed to get a harvest”). Financial stress that makes a quick answer appealing.
client_words: If I give enough, God has to bless me financially.
My giving is an investment with God.
If I’m still struggling, I didn’t give enough.
God owes me for what I’ve given.
The more I give, the richer I should get.
I give so that I’ll get.

beliefs.belief: My words create my reality, so I must ‘name it and claim it.’
beliefs.origins: Teaching that faith-filled words have power to bring health, wealth, or success. Fear that saying something negative will make it happen.
client_words: If I say it with enough faith, it will happen.
Saying something negative will make it come true.
I have to claim my healing even if I’m still sick.
My confession controls my future.
I can’t admit I’m struggling, or I’ll make it worse.
God has to do what I declare.

beliefs.belief: If God doesn’t do a miracle, He doesn’t care.
beliefs.origins: Praying desperately for a miracle that did not come. Losing someone you begged God to save.
client_words: If God loved me, He would have fixed this.
God helps other people but not me.
My prayers don’t matter to Him.
Unanswered prayer means God doesn’t care.
God has abandoned me.
I can’t trust a God who says no.

beliefs.belief: God’s blessing always shows up as health and wealth.
beliefs.origins: Prosperity preaching that equates faith with financial success and good health. Social media that shows Christians’ blessings mainly as money, homes, and comfort.
client_words: If I were blessed, I’d be healthy and comfortable.
Poor or sick Christians must be doing something wrong.
God is blessing others, but not me.
Money shows how much God loves me.
My struggles mean I’m out of God’s favor.
Real blessing is material.

beliefs.belief: Good Christians don’t have problems.
beliefs.origins: Growing up in a family that hid its problems to look good at church. Hearing testimonies that ended with “and now everything is wonderful.” Being told that troubles mean you are out of God’s will.
client_words: If I were a better Christian, I wouldn’t have these problems.
I have to look like I have it all together.
Other Christians don’t struggle like I do.
My problems prove I’m failing God.
I can’t tell anyone at church what’s really going on.
Real faith makes life easy.

beliefs.belief: My worth depends on how much I serve.
beliefs.origins: Being praised mainly for being helpful or useful as a child. A church culture that celebrated the busiest volunteers.
client_words: I’m only valuable when I’m helping.
If I stop serving, no one will want me.
I have to say yes to every request.
Rest is selfish.
God loves people who do more for Him.
My busyness proves my faithfulness.

beliefs.belief: My needs and feelings never count.
beliefs.origins: Teaching about self-denial that left no room for your own needs. A home where your feelings were ignored, dismissed, or punished.
client_words: My needs don’t matter.
It’s selfish to want anything for myself.
I shouldn’t bother anyone with how I feel.
Other people always come first.
If I have needs, I’m being weak.
God doesn’t care about my feelings.

beliefs.belief: God is like my father (or mother).
beliefs.origins: Childhood experiences with a parent who was harsh, distant, critical, absent, unpredictable, or abusive. Learning about God mainly through how your parents treated you.
client_words: God is distant, just like my dad was.
God is always angry, like my father.
God is never satisfied, like my mother.
God will leave, like my parent did.
I can’t trust God because I couldn’t trust my parents.
God is unpredictable, like the people who raised me.

beliefs.belief: Enjoying life is worldly or sinful.
beliefs.origins: A strict religious upbringing that frowned on fun, laughter, music, or celebration. Hearing that pleasure leads to sin.
client_words: Having fun is unspiritual.
If I enjoy something, I should feel guilty.
Real Christians are serious all the time.
Pleasure always leads to sin.
God wants me to be miserable to stay holy.
Laughing and celebrating are worldly.

beliefs.belief: Doubt means I am not a real Christian.
beliefs.origins: Being told that questions or doubts are sinful. A church culture where everyone seemed certain.
