client_words: If I have doubts, I must not really believe.
Real Christians never question anything.
God is angry with me for doubting.
I can’t tell anyone about my doubts.
My doubts prove I was never saved.
If I can’t answer every question, my faith is fake.

beliefs.belief: If I don’t feel close to God, He has left me.
beliefs.origins: Times of spiritual dryness after seasons of closeness. Depression or grief that dulls all feelings, including spiritual ones.
client_words: God has abandoned me.
I can’t feel Him, so He must be gone.
I must have done something to drive Him away.
Other people feel God, but I don’t.
My prayers just hit the ceiling.
God is close to others, not to me.

beliefs.belief: Faith means never asking questions.
beliefs.origins: Being told to “just believe” when you asked honest questions as a child. Leaders who treated questions as rebellion.
client_words: Asking questions means I don’t trust God.
Good Christians just accept everything.
If I start asking, I’ll lose my faith.
God is offended by my questions.
Thinking too much is dangerous.
I shouldn’t need to understand.

beliefs.belief: My faith is only as strong as my feelings.
beliefs.origins: Church experiences that focused on emotional highs. Feeling spiritually strong only after retreats, worship nights, or revivals.
client_words: I don’t feel anything, so my faith must be weak.
I’m only close to God when I feel it.
My faith comes and goes with my mood.
If I don’t feel excited, I must be backsliding.
Real faith always feels strong.
I need another spiritual high.

beliefs.belief: Real faith means never feeling afraid.
beliefs.origins: Hearing “Fear not” verses used to shame you for feeling afraid. Anxiety that feels like spiritual failure.
client_words: If I had real faith, I wouldn’t be afraid.
My anxiety is a sin.
God is disappointed when I’m scared.
I have to hide my fear from other Christians.
Being afraid means I don’t trust God.
Strong Christians are never anxious.

beliefs.belief: I’m not good enough to go to heaven.
beliefs.origins: Believing heaven is a reward for good people. Deep awareness of your own sins and failures.
client_words: Heaven is for good people, not people like me.
I’ve done too much wrong to go to heaven.
I’ll never be holy enough.
God might let others in, but not me.
I have to become a better person first.
I don’t deserve heaven.

beliefs.belief: My loved one in heaven is watching me and is disappointed in me.
beliefs.origins: Guilt about things left unsaid or undone before your loved one died. A parent or grandparent who was often critical while alive.
client_words: Mom is watching me and shaking her head.
Dad would be so disappointed in me.
I let them down, and now they know everything.
They’re upset I didn’t visit more.
I have to live up to what they wanted.
They see every mistake I make.

beliefs.belief: Heaven will be an endless, boring church service.
beliefs.origins: Pictures of heaven as clouds, harps, and endless singing. Long, dull church services in childhood.
client_words: Heaven sounds boring.
I’d rather stay on earth.
Forever singing hymns? No thanks.
I’ll miss all the good things here.
Eternity will feel like it never ends, in a bad way.
I feel guilty that heaven doesn’t excite me.

beliefs.belief: In heaven I’ll be grieving for the people who aren’t there.
beliefs.origins: Loving family members or friends who do not follow Christ. Fear that heaven cannot be happy if they are missing.
client_words: I can’t be happy in heaven without them.
Heaven will feel empty if they’re not there.
I’ll spend eternity missing someone.
How can God expect me to rejoice?
Heaven can’t be perfect if people I love are lost.
I’d rather not think about heaven at all.

beliefs.belief: In heaven every mistake I made will be shown to everyone.
beliefs.origins: Teaching or stories about a “movie” of your life shown in heaven. Shame about secret sins or past failures.
client_words: Everyone in heaven will see my worst moments.
I’ll be humiliated in front of everyone.
My secret sins will be shown on a big screen.
I’ll be ashamed forever.
People will think less of me in heaven.
God will embarrass me for what I did.

beliefs.belief: Every sinful thought puts me in danger of hell.
beliefs.origins: Frightening sermons about hell that focused on single sins. A sensitive or anxious conscience that treats every thought as a crisis.
client_words: One bad thought and I could be lost.
I have to watch every thought or I’ll go to hell.
God is ready to condemn me for what crossed my mind.
My mind is so sinful, I can’t be saved.
I can’t relax, or I’ll slip.
Every thought is a test I might fail.

beliefs.belief: If I die with an unconfessed sin, I will go to hell.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that forgiveness only covers sins you specifically confess. Fear of dying suddenly before you can confess.
client_words: I have to confess every sin or I’ll be lost.
What if I forget one?
If I die suddenly, I might go to hell.
I can never relax until I’ve confessed everything.
My salvation depends on my confession list.
One missed sin could cost me heaven.

beliefs.belief: I’m going to hell because of my many sins.
beliefs.origins: A long history of sin, addiction, or broken relationships. Shame that has grown over many years.
client_words: I’ve done too much; hell is where I belong.
My sins are too many to count.
God could never take someone like me.
It’s too late for me.
I deserve hell, so that’s where I’m going.
Grace is for better people.

beliefs.belief: My loved one is in hell because I didn’t share my faith enough.
beliefs.origins: Grief over a loved one who died without clear faith. Teaching that placed the full weight of someone’s salvation on your witness.
client_words: It’s my fault they’re lost.
If I had said more, they’d be in heaven.
God holds me responsible for their soul.
I failed them forever.
I can never forgive myself for staying quiet.
Their eternity rested on me.

beliefs.belief: Fear of hell is the main reason to follow God.
beliefs.origins: Coming to faith mainly through frightening sermons about hell. Teaching that used fear to motivate obedience.
client_words: I follow God so I don’t go to hell.
If I weren’t afraid, I’d stop obeying.
God is mainly someone to avoid angering.
Love is nice, but fear is what keeps me in line.
I don’t really enjoy God; I just fear Him.
Fear is the only thing that works for me.

beliefs.belief: My body doesn’t matter to God; only my soul counts.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that focused only on “saving souls.” Ideas that the body is a prison and the spirit is what really matters. Neglecting health, rest, or care because it seemed unspiritual.
client_words: Only my soul matters to God.
Taking care of my body is unspiritual.
My body is just a shell.
It doesn’t matter how I treat my body.
God only cares about spiritual things.
My physical needs aren’t important.

beliefs.belief: After death we become spirits floating forever.
beliefs.origins: Cartoons and movies showing people as ghosts on clouds. Funeral sayings that focus only on the soul.
client_words: We’ll just be spirits in the sky.
Eternity sounds empty and unreal.
I won’t have a body anymore.
Heaven will be vague and shadowy.
The physical world doesn’t matter forever.
I can’t imagine what forever will be like.

beliefs.belief: My illness, disability, or scars will last forever.
beliefs.origins: Living with chronic illness, pain, or disability. Physical scars from injury, surgery, or abuse.
client_words: I’ll always be like this.
My body will never be whole.
My scars define me forever.
There’s no hope for my body.
Heaven won’t change this.
I’ll carry this pain forever.

beliefs.belief: If my body is cremated, God can’t raise it.
beliefs.origins: Worry about a loved one who was cremated. Teaching that cremation is forbidden or makes resurrection impossible.
client_words: My loved one can’t be raised because of cremation.
God needs the whole body to raise it.
I made the wrong choice for my loved one.
Cremation ruins resurrection.
God won’t be able to find all the pieces.
My body has to be preserved for God to raise it.

beliefs.belief: I won’t know my loved ones after the resurrection.
beliefs.origins: Grief over someone you deeply miss. Hearing that in heaven we will be so focused on God that we won’t know anyone.
client_words: I’ll never see my loved one again.
We won’t recognize each other.
Our relationship will be gone in heaven.
Heaven will feel lonely without them.
We’ll be strangers.
My love for them won’t matter anymore.

beliefs.belief: If I grieve deeply, I don’t trust God.
beliefs.origins: Hearing “They’re in a better place, so don’t be sad.” A church culture that expects quick recovery from loss. Feeling pressure to look strong for others.
client_words: If I really trusted God, I wouldn’t be this sad.
I should be over this by now.
My tears show weak faith.
I have to be strong for everyone.
Christians shouldn’t grieve this much.
I’m letting God down by hurting so badly.

beliefs.belief: God took my loved one because He needed them more than I did.
beliefs.origins: Comforting sayings at funerals: “God needed another angel” or “God needed them more.” Searching for a reason behind a painful loss. Feeling that God chose against you.
client_words: God needed them more than I did.
God chose to take them from me.
God must not care about my pain.
I wasn’t important enough to keep them.
God wanted them in heaven, so He took them.
I’m angry at God for taking them.

beliefs.belief: Being afraid of death means my faith is weak.
beliefs.origins: Hearing that Christians should welcome death without fear. Anxiety about dying, illness, or the unknown.
client_words: If I had real faith, I wouldn’t be afraid to die.
My fear proves I’m not sure of heaven.
Good Christians are excited to die.
I’m ashamed of being afraid.
I can’t admit this fear to anyone.
My fear must mean I’m not saved.

beliefs.belief: My loved one who died by suicide can never be with God.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that suicide is an unforgivable sin. Fear that because there was no chance to repent, salvation was lost.
client_words: They can’t be in heaven because of how they died.
Suicide is the one sin God won’t forgive.
They didn’t have time to repent, so they’re lost.
I’ll never see them again.
I should have stopped them.
God rejected them in their worst moment.

beliefs.belief: My loved one died because I didn’t pray enough.
beliefs.origins: Praying hard for someone who still died. Teaching that enough prayer always brings healing.
client_words: If I had prayed more, they would still be alive.
It’s my fault God didn’t heal them.
My prayers weren’t good enough.
I failed them when it mattered most.
God was waiting for me to pray harder.
I’ll never forgive myself.

beliefs.belief: If my prayer isn’t answered, I prayed the wrong way.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that the right words, faith, or method guarantee answers. Long-awaited prayers that haven’t been answered the way you hoped.
client_words: I must have said it wrong.
If I had more faith, God would have answered.
God answers other people, but not me.
There must be a secret to prayer I’m missing.
My prayers don’t work.
It’s my fault God said no.

beliefs.belief: God only listens if I use the right words.
beliefs.origins: Hearing others pray eloquently and feeling yours are too plain. Being taught formal or set prayers as the only proper way.
client_words: My prayers aren’t good enough.
I don’t know how to pray right.
Other people’s prayers sound better.
If I say it wrong, God won’t hear.
I need special words for God to listen.
I’m too embarrassed to pray out loud.

beliefs.belief: Asking God more than once shows a lack of faith.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that you should pray once and then “claim it.” Fear that repeating a request shows doubt. Feeling like a nuisance to God.
client_words: I already asked, so asking again shows doubt.
God is tired of hearing about this.
I should just trust and stop asking.
Repeating myself is nagging God.
If I believed, once would be enough.
God will be annoyed if I keep praying.

beliefs.belief: If I pray enough, I shouldn’t need a doctor or counselor.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that seeking medical or psychological help shows weak faith. Stories of healing through prayer alone.
client_words: If I pray enough, I won’t need help.
Seeing a doctor means I don’t trust God.
Counseling is for people with weak faith.
God will be disappointed if I get treatment.
My prayers should be enough.
Taking medicine is giving up on God.

beliefs.belief: God only hears the prayers of good people.
beliefs.origins: Feeling too sinful or unworthy to pray. Verses about God hearing “the righteous” read as “perfect people only.” Comparing yourself with people who seem holier.
client_words: God won’t listen to someone like me.
I have to be good before I can pray.
My sins block my prayers.
God only hears holy people.
I’m too far gone for God to hear me.
I’ll pray when I get my life together.

beliefs.belief: If I don’t read my Bible every day, God is displeased with me.
beliefs.origins: Strict devotional checklists from church or youth group. Guilt when you miss a day or fall behind on a reading plan.
client_words: I missed a day, so God is disappointed.
I’m a bad Christian because I don’t read enough.
I have to finish my reading plan or I’ve failed.
God only blesses me when I’ve done my devotions.
I can’t pray until I’ve read my chapter.
Missing Bible reading means God is far from me.

beliefs.belief: Every verse applies directly to me, whatever its context.
beliefs.origins: Reading single verses on calendars, mugs, and social media. Devotionals that use verses without their setting.
client_words: This verse is God speaking directly to my situation.
I don’t need to know the background.
If I open my Bible randomly, God will show me what to do.
Every warning in the Bible is about me.
Context doesn’t matter; God’s Word is God’s Word.
That promise means God will do exactly this for me.

beliefs.belief: I must never question or wrestle with hard passages.
beliefs.origins: Being told to “just accept it” when you asked about difficult verses. Fear that questioning the Bible means doubting God.
client_words: Questioning the Bible is sinful.
If a passage troubles me, something is wrong with my faith.
I should just ignore the hard parts.
Good Christians understand everything.
Asking about this will make me lose my faith.
I’m not allowed to be confused.

beliefs.belief: Any verse is a promise I can claim for whatever I want.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that encourages “claiming” verses for health, wealth, or success. Popular verses on posters taken out of context.
client_words: God promised this, so He has to do it.
I’m claiming this verse for my situation.
If it didn’t happen, I didn’t claim it right.
Every verse is a promise to me.
Philippians 4:13 means I can do anything I want.
God owes me what the verse says.

beliefs.belief: Only pastors or scholars can understand the Bible.
beliefs.origins: Feeling intimidated by the Bible’s size, history, or language. Church settings where only leaders explained Scripture.
client_words: I’m not smart enough to understand the Bible.
I need a pastor to tell me what it means.
The Bible is too hard for ordinary people.
I’ll just get it wrong.
Only experts should read it seriously.
I don’t have enough education.

beliefs.belief: Questioning my pastor is questioning God.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that the pastor speaks for God and must not be challenged. Leaders who used verses about authority to silence concerns.
client_words: If I question my pastor, I’m rebelling against God.
My pastor can’t be wrong.
Raising concerns is gossip or division.
God will punish me for disagreeing with a leader.
I just need to submit and stay quiet.
Good church members never ask questions.

beliefs.belief: Pastors and leaders are closer to God than I am.
beliefs.origins: Seeing leaders on a stage and feeling distant from them. Church cultures that treat clergy as a higher class of Christian.
client_words: Pastors have a special connection to God that I don’t.
God listens to leaders more than me.
I’m just an ordinary church member.
My prayers don’t count as much as theirs.
I need a leader to hear from God for me.
I’ll never be as close to God as they are.

beliefs.belief: Leaving a church means leaving God.
beliefs.origins: Being told that anyone who leaves is backsliding or rebellious. Deep loyalty to a church family.
client_words: If I leave, God will leave me.
Leaving means I’m rebelling against God.
My faith depends on this church.
I’ll lose God if I lose these people.
God will punish me for leaving.
There’s no other place for me to worship.

beliefs.belief: Family problems must be kept secret to protect the church.
beliefs.origins: Being told not to “air dirty laundry” or hurt the church’s reputation. Pressure to protect a leader or respected family.
client_words: If I tell anyone, I’ll hurt the church.
We have to look like a good Christian family.
Talking about this would be gossip.
God wants me to protect our reputation.
It’s disloyal to ask for help.
If I speak up, I’ll be blamed.

beliefs.belief: Being busy at church means being spiritual.
beliefs.origins: A church culture that praises the people who do the most. Feeling guilty when you say no to a ministry.
client_words: The more I do at church, the more spiritual I am.
If I step back, I’m letting God down.
Busy Christians are the best Christians.
I don’t have time to rest; there’s too much ministry.
My worth comes from my church roles.
Saying no is unspiritual.

beliefs.belief: Being submissive means accepting mistreatment or abuse.
beliefs.origins: Teaching about submission without the matching teaching about how husbands must love. A spouse or leader who used Scripture to demand obedience.
client_words: God wants me to put up with this.
If I leave or tell anyone, I’m disobeying God.
It’s my fault for not being submissive enough.
A good wife (or husband) endures anything.
Speaking up would dishonor my spouse.
I have no right to be safe.

beliefs.belief: Because I am divorced, God can’t use me.
beliefs.origins: Church policies that kept divorced people from serving. Shame or judgment from other Christians.
client_words: I’m damaged goods.
God can’t use someone who failed at marriage.
I’m a second-class Christian now.
My divorce disqualifies me forever.
I have nothing to offer God.
Everyone at church sees me as a failure.

beliefs.belief: Sex is dirty, even in marriage.
beliefs.origins: Growing up where sex was never discussed, or only talked about as shameful. Strict warnings before marriage that did not change after the wedding.
client_words: Sex is something to be ashamed of.
Good Christians shouldn’t enjoy sex.
I feel guilty after intimacy with my spouse.
Desire is sinful, even in marriage.
God looks away from that part of our lives.
My body is dirty.

beliefs.belief: If my children turn away from God, I failed as a parent.
beliefs.origins: Reading Proverbs 22:6 as a guarantee. Comments from others that blame parents.
client_words: It’s my fault my child left the faith.
If I had been a better parent, they’d still believe.
Proverbs 22:6 proves I failed.
Everyone at church blames me.
God is disappointed in my parenting.
There’s no hope for my child.

beliefs.belief: Single people are less complete in God’s eyes.
beliefs.origins: Church activities built mostly around couples and families. Questions like “When are you getting married?” Feeling left out or invisible.
client_words: I’m incomplete without a spouse.
God loves married people more.
My life won’t really start until I’m married.
Something must be wrong with me.
Single people don’t fit in the church.
God has forgotten me.

beliefs.belief: If I miss God’s perfect will, my life is ruined.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that God has one exact plan and missing it means settling for second best forever. Regret over a past decision, such as a job, a move, or a marriage.
client_words: I made the wrong choice, and now my life is ruined.
I’ve missed God’s plan forever.
I’m stuck with second best.
God can’t fix this now.
If I make the wrong decision, everything is over.
I’ll never get back on track.

beliefs.belief: God’s will is always the thing I least want.
beliefs.origins: Fear that God will send you somewhere you dread if you surrender to Him. Teaching that emphasized sacrifice without joy.
client_words: If I want it, God probably doesn’t.
God will make me do what I hate.
Surrendering to God means losing everything I love.
God’s plan is always the hardest path.
My desires don’t matter to God.
God likes to make me uncomfortable.

beliefs.belief: I need a clear sign from God before I can decide anything.
beliefs.origins: Stories like Gideon’s fleece used as a model for every decision. Fear of making a mistake.
client_words: I can’t move until God shows me clearly.
Without a sign, I might choose wrong.
God hasn’t spoken, so I’ll wait.
Everyone else gets clear signs except me.
If I decide without a sign, I’m not trusting God.
I’m stuck until I’m certain.

beliefs.belief: Every decision has one right answer, and I must find it.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that God has a specific choice for everything, down to what you eat. Perfectionism and fear of mistakes.
client_words: There’s only one right choice, and I have to find it.
If I choose wrong, God will be displeased.
I can’t decide until I’m sure it’s the perfect choice.
Every little decision matters eternally.
I keep second-guessing everything.
Other people always know the right answer.

beliefs.belief: If something is hard, it can’t be God’s will.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that God’s will always feels peaceful and easy. Using “closed doors” as the only sign of God’s leading.
client_words: If it’s this hard, God must not be in it.
God’s will should feel easy.
Difficulty means I took a wrong turn.
I should quit because it’s hard.
A closed door always means no.
If I were in God’s will, everything would go smoothly.

beliefs.belief: If I am suffering, God is punishing me.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that every hardship is God’s punishment for sin. Friends who asked, “What did you do to deserve this?” A guilty conscience that looks for reasons.
client_words: God is punishing me for something.
I must have done something to deserve this.
This pain proves God is angry with me.
If I were living right, this wouldn’t happen.
I have to figure out what sin caused this.
God wants me to suffer.

beliefs.belief: Real Christians don’t suffer.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that faith brings a trouble-free life. Prosperity messages that promise health and success.
client_words: If I were a real Christian, I wouldn’t be going through this.
My suffering proves my faith is fake.
Other Christians don’t suffer like I do.
God promised me an easy life.
Something is wrong with my faith.
Faith should protect me from pain.

beliefs.belief: I must figure out the reason for everything bad that happens.
beliefs.origins: A need for control and certainty. Anxiety that searches for answers to feel safe.
client_words: I can’t rest until I know why this happened.
There must be a reason, and I have to find it.
If I understood, I could accept it.
Not knowing means God doesn’t care.
I keep replaying it looking for answers.
Other people seem to understand their suffering.

beliefs.belief: Complaining to God is a sin.
beliefs.origins: Verses about not grumbling applied to all honest prayer. Being told to always be thankful and never sad.
client_words: I shouldn’t tell God I’m upset.
Good Christians never complain.
God will be angry if I’m honest.
I have to pretend I’m fine when I pray.
Questioning God is rebellion.
I should only thank Him, never vent.

beliefs.belief: My suffering means God has abandoned me.
beliefs.origins: Long seasons of pain without relief. Prayers that seem unanswered.
client_words: God has left me alone in this.
If God were with me, I wouldn’t be suffering.
God has forgotten me.
No one, not even God, cares.
I’m on my own now.
God gave up on me.

beliefs.belief: I must keep the rules to stay in God’s favor.
beliefs.origins: A legalistic church background with long lists of do’s and don’ts. A home where approval depended on obedience.
client_words: One slip and I lose God’s favor.
God only likes me when I follow the rules.
I have to keep earning God’s approval.
My standing with God depends on my behavior.
If I break a rule, God turns away.
I need more rules to stay safe.

beliefs.belief: The more I do for God, the more He loves me.
beliefs.origins: A home where affection came through achievement. Church recognition for the most active members.
client_words: God loves me more when I serve more.
If I slow down, God will love me less.
I have to keep proving my love to God.
Busy Christians are God’s favorites.
My worth is measured by my service.
God’s love has to be earned.

beliefs.belief: Because of grace, my choices don’t matter.
beliefs.origins: Reacting against legalism by swinging to the other extreme. Hearing “God will forgive anyway” used to excuse sin.
client_words: God will forgive me anyway, so it doesn’t matter.
Grace means I don’t have to change.
My choices don’t affect my relationship with God.
Obedience is legalism.
I can live however I want.
Sin doesn’t really hurt anyone.

beliefs.belief: Resting or receiving help means I’m spiritually lazy.
beliefs.origins: A strong work ethic taught as a measure of godliness. Feeling guilty when you sit still.
client_words: Resting is lazy.
I should be doing more for God.
I can’t accept help; I should help others.
If I stop, everything will fall apart.
Needing help means I’m weak.
God is disappointed when I take a break.

beliefs.belief: I have to clean up my life before I can come to God.
beliefs.origins: Feeling too ashamed or messy to approach God. Church cultures where people seemed to have it all together.
client_words: I need to get my life together first.
God won’t accept me as I am.
Once I stop this habit, I’ll come back to God.
I’m too messy for church.
I have to earn my way back.
God only wants people who have it together.

beliefs.belief: I should live in constant fear of the end times.
beliefs.origins: Frightening movies, books, or sermons about the end of the world. Childhood fear of being left behind.
client_words: The end of the world terrifies me.
Every news story makes me panic.
I can’t enjoy life because the end might come.
I should be afraid if I’m taking this seriously.
Something terrible is about to happen.
I can’t stop thinking about the end times.

beliefs.belief: Current events tell me exactly when the end is coming.
beliefs.origins: Prophecy teachers who connect news headlines to specific dates. Past predictions that seemed convincing.
client_words: This event proves the end is next year.
I’ve figured out the timeline.
I need to watch the news for every sign.
The experts have calculated the date.
If I miss the signs, I’ll be caught off guard.
I can’t make plans because the end is so close.

beliefs.belief: I could be left behind because I’m not good enough.
beliefs.origins: Movies and books about being left behind. Childhood panic when family members could not be found.
client_words: When Jesus comes, I’ll be left behind.
I’m not holy enough to be taken.
I panic when I can’t find my family.
One sin could make me miss it.
I have to be good enough to be ready.
God will leave me because of my failures.

beliefs.belief: Since the world is ending, planning for the future doesn’t matter.
beliefs.origins: Teaching that the end is so near that education, savings, or careers are pointless. Discouragement or hopelessness about the world.
client_words: Why plan when the world is ending?
Saving money is pointless.
Education and careers don’t matter anymore.
I don’t need to take care of my health or future.
Only spiritual things are worth doing now.
There’s no point in starting anything long-term.

beliefs.belief: Natural disasters are God punishing the people they strike.
beliefs.origins: Public figures who blame disasters on the sins of certain groups. Teaching that every tragedy is a direct judgment.
client_words: Those people must have deserved it.
God sent that disaster to punish them.
If a disaster hits me, God is angry with me.
Tragedies always mean judgment.
I can tell who God is punishing by what happens to them.
Victims should examine what they did wrong.

beliefs.belief: Something is wrong with me.
beliefs.origins: This belief often starts early. A child who is criticized, compared, ignored, teased, or treated as a problem can conclude, “The trouble must be me.” Painful experiences such as abuse, rejection, divorce, or a parent’s anger can leave the same message, because children tend to blame themselves for what adults do.
client_words: Other people seem normal; I am not.
If people really knew me, they would see what is wrong with me.
I always mess things up because I am broken.
Everyone else got something I was born without.
When things go wrong, it must be my fault.
I have to hide the real me.

beliefs.belief: I am worthless.
beliefs.origins: Many people learn this belief from the way they were treated: being called names, put down, ignored, used, or compared unfavorably with others. When love depended on grades, looks, money, or behavior, a child can conclude that a person is only worth what he or she produces.
client_words: I am not worth anything.
Other people matter; I don’t.
If I disappeared, no one would notice.
I have nothing to offer.
I only matter when I am useful.
I don’t deserve good things.

beliefs.belief: I am not lovable.
beliefs.origins: This belief often grows out of love that was missing, inconsistent, or conditional. A parent who was cold, absent, harsh, or only affectionate when we behaved well can leave the impression that we are hard to love.
client_words: If people really knew me, they would not love me.
I am too much, or not enough, to be loved.
Love always runs out for me.
I have to earn every bit of affection.
People only put up with me.
Even God must find me hard to love.

beliefs.belief: I am a failure.
beliefs.origins: This belief often comes from high expectations, harsh criticism, or being compared with brothers, sisters, or classmates. It can take root after a major setback such as a divorce, a business loss, a lost job, or a broken promise to ourselves.
client_words: I never get anything right.
Everyone else succeeds; I don’t.
Why try? I will only fail again.
I have wasted my life.
I let everyone down.
One mistake ruins everything.

beliefs.belief: I am powerless.
beliefs.origins: People often learn powerlessness in situations where they truly had no control: growing up with an abusive or addicted parent, being bullied, living through poverty or illness, or being trapped in a controlling relationship. The lesson “nothing I do makes a difference” can follow a person into adulthood, even after…
client_words: Nothing I do makes a difference.
Things just happen to me.
I have no say in my own life.
Other people control everything.
I can’t change anything.
Why bother trying?

beliefs.belief: I cannot handle this.
beliefs.origins: This belief often appears when stress piles up: illness, caring for a loved one, money problems, grief, or several crises at once. It can also come from growing up without being allowed to face difficulties, or from being overwhelmed as a child with burdens too heavy for a child to carry.
client_words: This is too much for me.
I’m going to fall apart.
I can’t cope with one more thing.
Other people could handle this, but not me.
I need to escape.
If this goes on, I’ll break.

beliefs.belief: I cannot make it on my own.
beliefs.origins: This belief can develop when a person was overprotected, never allowed to make decisions, or told they were incapable. It can also follow years of depending on a spouse, parent, or caregiver, or a loss that left someone suddenly alone.
client_words: I need someone to take care of me.
I can’t make decisions on my own.
If I lose this person, I’ll fall apart.
I’m not capable of running my life.
I’ll put up with anything rather than be alone.
Others know better than I do.

beliefs.belief: I don’t belong.
beliefs.origins: Feeling like an outsider can come from moving often, being left out at school, growing up in a family where we felt different, or being excluded because of our background, looks, or abilities. Some people felt unwanted at home or were treated as the “odd one.” Later, the belief can make us hold back in groups, read…
client_words: I never fit in anywhere.
Everyone else has their group.
People just tolerate me.
I’m always on the outside looking in.
If I speak up, they’ll see I don’t belong.
I’m different from everyone.

beliefs.belief: People will leave me.
beliefs.origins: Fear of being left often begins with real loss: a parent who left, died, or was emotionally absent; a divorce; repeated moves; or a partner who walked away. A child may conclude that people always leave, and that it must be because of something in them.
client_words: Everyone I love eventually leaves.
It’s only a matter of time.
If I let someone close, they’ll abandon me.
I have to keep people happy or they’ll go.
I’m easy to walk away from.
I can’t survive being left again.

beliefs.belief: No one will care for me when I need them.
beliefs.origins: This belief often starts in homes where needs were ignored, dismissed, or punished, or where a child had to care for a parent instead of being cared for. Times of illness, crisis, or grief when no one showed up can deepen it.
client_words: If I fall apart, no one will be there.
I have to take care of myself because no one else will.
Asking for help is pointless.
People only show up when they need something.
My needs are a burden to others.
I’m on my own.

beliefs.belief: Nobody loves me.
beliefs.origins: This belief can grow from a childhood without warmth or affection, the loss of a spouse or parent, a painful breakup, or long seasons of loneliness. Depression can also color everything gray, so that even real love is hard to feel.
client_words: No one cares about me.
If I died, no one would miss me.
Everyone else is loved but me.
People are nice to me only out of obligation.
I’m completely alone.
Even God doesn’t love me.

beliefs.belief: People cannot be trusted.
beliefs.origins: This belief usually comes from betrayal: a parent who broke promises, abuse by someone who should have protected us, a spouse’s unfaithfulness, gossip, or being cheated. After being hurt, it makes sense to protect ourselves.
client_words: Everyone has a hidden agenda.
If I trust, I’ll get hurt.
People always let you down.
I can only count on myself.
Kindness is just a setup.
It’s safer to keep everyone at arm’s length.

beliefs.belief: My needs don’t matter.
beliefs.origins: Many people learn this in families where their needs were ignored, mocked, or treated as selfish, or where they had to take care of a parent or siblings. Some were praised for always putting others first, so they learned that having needs was bad.
client_words: Other people’s needs come first, always.
It’s selfish to want anything for myself.
I don’t want to be a bother.
I can rest when everything else is done.
If I say no, people will be upset.
My feelings aren’t important.

beliefs.belief: Things will always go badly.
beliefs.origins: This belief often follows a long run of hardship: repeated losses, chronic illness, financial struggles, or a childhood where good things rarely lasted. When disappointment comes again and again, the mind learns to expect it, partly to avoid being caught off guard.
client_words: Nothing ever works out for me.
As soon as things get better, something will ruin it.
Why hope? It never turns out.
My life is just one bad thing after another.
Good things don’t last.
It will always be like this.

beliefs.belief: The world is unsafe.
beliefs.origins: This belief often comes from real danger: abuse, violence, a frightening accident, a crime, a natural disaster, or growing up in a chaotic home. Constant news of tragedy can strengthen it.
client_words: Something bad could happen at any moment.
I have to stay on guard.
It’s not safe to go out.
People are dangerous.
If I relax, I’ll get hurt.
Nowhere is safe.

beliefs.belief: Something terrible is going to happen.
beliefs.origins: A sense of coming doom often follows a sudden shock, such as an unexpected death, diagnosis, or accident, which teaches the mind that disaster can strike without warning. It can also grow in homes where parents were constantly worried, or where something bad really did happen often.
client_words: I just know something bad is coming.
If I stop worrying, it will happen.
Every phone call might be bad news.
Things are too good; something will go wrong.
I need to be prepared for the worst.
I can’t shake this feeling of dread.

beliefs.belief: I must be perfect.
beliefs.origins: Perfectionism often grows in homes where love or approval seemed to depend on performance, where mistakes were criticized harshly, or where a child tried to keep chaos at bay by being “good.” Schools, sports, workplaces, and even churches can reward it. Perfectionism can look like high standards, but underneath is…
client_words: If it isn’t perfect, it’s a failure.
I can’t let anyone see my flaws.
I have to do it all myself so it’s done right.
Good enough isn’t good enough.
If I make a mistake, people will think less of me.
I should be able to do better.

beliefs.belief: I must have everyone’s approval.
beliefs.origins: The need for approval often begins with parents whose love seemed conditional, frequent criticism, or rejection by peers. A child who learns that keeping others happy keeps them safe may grow into an adult who can’t say no, avoids conflict, and feels crushed by any disapproval.
client_words: If someone is upset with me, I’ve failed.
I can’t say no.
I need people to like me.
I worry constantly about what others think.
Criticism crushes me.
I’ll go along to keep the peace.

beliefs.belief: I must be in control.
beliefs.origins: The need for control often grows in chaotic or frightening homes, where a child tried to bring order by managing everything around them. It can also follow trauma, a sudden loss, or a time when things spun out of control.
client_words: If I don’t handle it, it will fall apart.
I can’t stand not knowing what will happen.
Others won’t do it right.
I have to plan for every possibility.
Letting go feels dangerous.
If I lose control, something bad will happen.

beliefs.belief: I must not make mistakes.
beliefs.origins: Fear of mistakes often comes from harsh punishment, ridicule, or anger when we got something wrong as children. Some families or schools treated every error as a character flaw.
client_words: Mistakes are unacceptable.
If I make a mistake, I’ll be humiliated.
I’d rather not try than get it wrong.
I go over things again and again to be sure.
One error can ruin everything.
I can’t forgive myself for mistakes.

beliefs.belief: It was my fault.
beliefs.origins: After abuse, an assault, an accident, a parent’s divorce, or a loved one’s death, many people blame themselves. Children especially assume they caused what happened, because it is less frightening than believing the adults around them were unsafe.
client_words: I should have stopped it.
If I had been better, it wouldn’t have happened.
I must have done something to cause it.
I deserved what happened.
I should have seen it coming.
It’s my fault they left.

beliefs.belief: What happened makes me dirty or bad.
beliefs.origins: This belief often follows sexual abuse, assault, betrayal, or humiliation. Shame can attach itself to the person who was hurt rather than to the person who did the harm.
client_words: I’m ruined.
No one would want me if they knew.
I feel dirty no matter what I do.
I’m damaged goods.
God must see me as stained.
What happened is who I am now.
